speechtext: With reference to the question which came up yesterday, and which was brought up by my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. J. D. Taylor) in regard to the inquiry made by Mr. Justice Murphy as commissioner to investigate frauds in the administration of the Chinese Act at Vancouver, I stated yesterday that I had a conference with the . Minister of Justice on the matter, but that I had had no time to read the report, and had only looked at the conclusions. The first conclusion is that Mr. Justice Murphy advises certain prosecutions be taken. The other recommendation was that the report should not be made public until the prosecutions had been taken, the reason being-I could not give the reason yesterday, but I can now-that if the report were made public before the prosecutions were undertaken, witnesses for the prosecution might disappear. I under-derstand, on further conference that the parties indicated for prosecution are in China and therefore that no prosecution we could undertake would reach them. I have looked at the report and see no reason why it should not be given to the public even in the face of the recommendations made by Mr. Justice Murphy. Therefore, I lav it on the table. speechtext: I wish to refer to a question asked by the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. J. D. Reid). I have made inquiries, and find that Mr. Courtrice applied for leave of absence without pay beginning on the 1st of July. He was granted the leave, but, on the reassembling of parliament he was told he must report for duty. He has been at work in the department at his ordinary duties since and including Wednesday afternoon.

I would like to ask my hon. friend the Minister of
Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) whether or not he has any further information about the alleged irregularities in connection with the census. I would like to inform him at the same time, that I have a letter from a gentleman residing in an apartment house in Toronto stating that people in that House to the number of twenty-two were not included in the enumeration. And when he asked the enumerator the reason for this, some very unsatisfactory reply was given, and the enumerator also stated that if any person were omitted they had enough in other respects to make up for any such losses. I have forgotten the exact expression, but it is something like that. I intended to bring the letter in, but omitted to do so. ' I do not know whether the minister has ascertained yet whether I have the honour to be enumerated or not. I would like very much to know.

I should have preferred not to make a statement until I had had an opportunity for fuller investigation. I hope the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) will send in the names of the people said to have been omitted, so that I may investigate the matter.
I will.

So far as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) himself is concerned I can only make a partial statement, not yet having had an opportunity to investigate the matter fully. The statement given me is that the enumerator called at the hon. gentleman's house when he and Mrs. Borden were out. The servant told him so and said that if he would come back, no doubt they would be in. The statement I have is that he went back five or six times, and was not able to find any body in the house. I am making more careful inquiry to find out whether that means that he w-as not able to find Mr. or Mrs. Borden, or that he was not able to find anybody at all. The statement made to me, was that he was not able to find any body at all. He did what his duty required in such circumstances and sent an absentee card to the office, which is in the office, and was there when my hon. friend made his statement the other day. That card will ensure that the case will be worked out and fully enumerated.

I made full inquiry, and my information is that the enumerator did state that he would call again, but from that time up to the present, so far as my information goes, h* never has called again. Of course, I havt. no personal knowledge of the matter, but that is the information that comes to me after careful inquiry.
Was the house open all the time?

The house has been open all the time.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext:
Before you leave the chair, I desire to refer briefly to the condition of matters in the northern district of Ontario as regards the preparation of the voters' lists for the unorganized portions. As the Prime Minister is aware, there was a good deal of discussion in the session of 1908 as to the methods which were prescribed by the then Election Act for the making up of the voters' lists, and a good deal of criticism was directed to the somewhat cumbrous procedure prescribed by the amendment to that Act. The amendment requires the services of a board of registration, comprising three judges chosen from the adjoining counties, the chairman of which was to be the senior judge of the electoral district for which the lists were to be made up. Now, I have received, as the sitting member, a semi-official noti-
9B01

9S02
fication that no voter' lists are to be made up under that Act, and that no board of registration is being constituted for that purpose. I am not aware, and my right hon. friend will be able to inform me, whether any special proclamation has been issued requiring the voters' lists in those unorganized territories under this Act to be made up at an earlier date than the period prescribed by the statute. If there has been no such proclamation, or if no such proclamation is to be made, then section 9a of the Act will govern, and the lists must be made up between two specified dates, namely, the 1st day of August and the 15th day of October in each year. Now since the discussion ensued upon the making up of these voters' lists a practical test of the workability of the Act has been made, it was made in the year 1908. I know that my right hon. friend will credit my words when I say that, with all the speed that could possibly be put upon the cumbrous machinery that was at the disposal of the district judges, by shortening the available time in a manner which was, according to my view, beyond the jurisdiction of the board of registration within those periods, from the first week in August up to the 26th day of October 1908, the judges were only able, with the kindly assistance of the Department of the Secretary of State, which opened the printing bureau on a Sunday and printed the lists, and then, by the kindly assistance of this government in sending a special train with the lists to the scene of the election, they were able, three hours after the election had commenced, three hours after the polls were opened, to get lists there, which were imperfect and irregular. During the course of revision by the board of registration there was a judgment written out by the board, of which I presume a copy is lodged in the office of the Secretary of State. It is not in my hand at the moment, but I can produce it shortly. The judgment was to the effect exactly as I contend, that under the provisions of this Act it was impossible, within the periods, and with the machinery at the control of the board, to revise and complete the lists within that time.
Now those are the conditions which prevailed in the northern districts in 1908. But the difficulties there are tremendously increased at the present time. There are polls, of which I have received a semi-official notification from the enumerator, which will be opened in the district of West Algoma, to get to which, and to get back again to my home, will require a, journey of not less than 2,000 miles. Now what I am told is that the board of registration will have to be a law unto selves that in making this Act workable and applying it to the preparation of these
lists, they are going to cut down all the periods mentioned in the Ontario Voters' Act which governs the period for making up the list under this Act. Consequently the lists cannot be properly prepared.
If the enumeration is to take place fifteen days after the notice, or ten days after the notice, as the case may be, there will hardly be time to enable anybody to get there in order to make the enumerator.
I am told that in some instances a cane* trip is required, and a great deal of walking and railway travel is necessary ia order to reach these polls. Therefore I draw this matteT to the attention of Uie government in order that, before the work of the board of registration is organized and the enumeration of the voters' in these polls is commenced, careful regard should be had to the condition of things which arose in 1908, and that care should be taken to give the necessary time in order that proper lists may be obtained, and that everybody may have an opportunity of seeing that fair lists are made and that a fair revision is had. The lists of 1908 were very unsatisfactory. Names were put upon these lists by the hundred, wthout any attempt to obtain information as regards the qualification of the voters.
That was shown to be the case before the Board of Registration, and in one place many hundreds of names were dropped off. The revision was not so satisfactory in other ridings where that contention was not expressly insisted upon. I should like the government to give some intimation as to whether, under that condition of the law, the Board of Registration is authorized by this Act to shorten the periods which are fixed for the making up of these lists. It is of the most vital importance if we are to have a fair list up there. It is all very well for an enumerator, after having given notice which, by the Act governing the time, is said to be thirty days, and which the Board of Registration reduced to ten days, to be there and get the names of a whole lot of men on a pay roll or from a mine superintendent or a road boss and put them on the list without giving an opportunity for any one to investigate. The Ontario Voters List Act, amended, of the Dominion Elections Act, is made to govern matters of this kind, provides that a longer time shall be prescribed for the making up of these lists. The section to which I refer reads as follows :
In the preparation of such lists the provisions of the law of the province regulating the preparation and manner of revising and bringing into force the provincial voters lists in the like cases shall, as far as possible, be observed and followed, but the revision of the said lists shall be had before Ihe board of ce-| gistration, who shall hear all appeals from the said enumerators, and no person whose name

is not included in the voters' lists so prepared and revised shall he entitled to vote.
Under the Ontario Consolidated Voters' Lists Act of 1907, section 60, not less than thirty days is the time prescribed for posting notices.
Not less than thirty days after the posting of the notices the enumerators shall visit every part of the territory where by the statute or by proclamation of the lieutenant governor there is required to be a polling place, and shall ascertain the names of all persons who are entitled to have their names entered on such lists, including any who may deliver to him an affidavit according to form 22a or 22b.
It is all very well for the enumerator to go to satisfy himself by reference, perhaps, to incorrect information as to the qualifications of voters, but there is a period prescribed by the Ontario Voters' Lists Act for the preparation and making up of these lists just the same as there is under the Assessment Act or in connection with any other procedure in an organized district. Especially is it necessary that sufficient time should be allowed in these remote districts, as we have to face them for the purpose of the preparation and revision of the voters' lists. The polls are absolutely new and are in very (recently opened up country and very remote and difficult of access. If the Board of Begistration is arbitrarily to be permitted to shorten the period from thirty days to ten days or even less, or to usurp authority not accorded to it by statute in order to make that change, there will be no accurate list of voters in the northern country, and there will be no opportunity afforded to any persons desirous of obtaining an accurate list by means of a fair revision of the list. The Act as originally framed provided that the time for appeal should be thirty days. That appeal has been cut down by the amendment of the Act to ten days. I am most anxious in the interest of a fair voters' list to be prepared under the most difficult conditions, to bring to the notice of the government the fact that if the Board of Registration is to arbitrarily change the law, arrogate to itself the functions of this government, revise and amend the statute and prescribe other days or sets of days and other times than those limited by this statute for the preparation of these lists, there will be greater confusion in that north country in connection with the preparation of these voters' lists than there was in 1908, more inconvenience and very great dissatisfaction with the methods which are employed in the making up of these lists.

speechtext:
When this Act was framed in 1908 my right hon. friend, with some hesitation, said that he hoped it would be workable. Strong objections were made by myself and others as to the workability of it, we having some personal knowledge of the local conditions, but I hope that my right hon. friend will realize that it is undesirable that the conditions to which I have referred shall again obtain in that part of the country.	.
It was stated by my right hon. friend that the act was intended to procure a fair voters' list, but I would refer him and his Minister of Justice to the proceedings and records of the Board of Registration to ascertain whether the provisions of the Act do provide for a fair voters' list. There is a ruling in writing by the Board, in which all members of the Board concur, that the proceedings necessary to procure proper lists under this Act could not be performed within the time and in the manner prescribed by the Act, and the Board went so far in the first instance as to say that the election then pending would have to be postponed in order that proper lists might be obtained. The Board, finding it had no power to interfere with the currency of the writ then issued, reconsidered their finding and decided to make a law unto themselves and to have a special train for the Board to carry its court from poll to poll to revise these lists. We know what confusion ensued; where the lists had to be sent down, the Secretary of State fetched from his constituency in a motor car, the printing bureau working on Sunday in violation of the Lord's Day Act and a special train sent out with the lists to Sault Ste. Marie, and along the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I desire that the government should give me this information: Has there been a proclamation under the Act of 1908 prescribing an earlier day for the making up of these voters' lists; if so, when will the work of enumeration be started and how long is it expected, from the most recent advice the government has, that it will take; and, will the government see to it that the Board of Registration is prevented in this instance from arrogating to itself the functions of government by abridging the time which by this Act is directed to be followed as far as possible. The words, 'as far as possible' are introduced into section 5 of the Act. But who can say that in a territory so vast that one has to travel
2,000	miles to go to and from these polls that the time limited by the Ontario Act is unfair.	Who will say that when in
order to get to a place to make up these lists one has to travel into an almost unknown region, that the thirty days prescribed by the Ontario Act for the preparation of the appeal and the holding of the Court, should, under the
difficult conditions existing, be curtailed, or any other period prescribed by the Board of Registration, to the prejudice of those who are anxious to have a fair list. This is a vital subject, and I would urge the government to consider the difficult conditions existing in that country, especially in West Algoma, where it is exceedingly difficult to get to these far distant polls where up to a year or two ago no white man's foot had ever stepped. In this territory, I have been told, that two or three thousand names are to be put on the lists. I can scarcely credit that. In the face of the imminence of a repetition of the various irregularities of procedure of 1908, I urge upon the government the very great necessity, in the interests of a fair election, of seeing that the procedure prescribed by the law is strictly followed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext:
The administration of the statute which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Boyce) has referred to is not in any way in the hands of the Department of Justice nor is it, I think, in the hands of any department of the government. The idea with which this statute was framed, and the intention of parliament in passing it, was that the preparation of the voters' lists in the unorganized portions of Ontario should be in the hands of the judges of the various courts of the districts constituting this unorganized territory, who were thought to be the best people for the practical administration of the provisions of the statute. The statute having been framed and passed with that intention it seems to me it is now in position to be worked out without reference to any kind of governmental supervision or control. The conditions which existed three years ago when this statute was for the first time coming into practical operation were of somewhat unusual character. Before, under the statute, it was possible to complete the lists the House was dissolved and a general election was called. That general election being fixed for the latter part of October and the lists being in preparation during the immediately preceding months it may very probably be that there was need, for limiting, to the very briefest period which the statute would permit, the times during which the various steps towards the preparation of a voters' list should be taken. The Secretary of State of that day did, I believe, concern himself to a very considerable extent, in an effort to be of assistance to the judges in working out the provisions of the Act. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Boyce) says that the practical operation of the statute at that time was in its result not satisfactory. That is probably a matter of opinion. At all events I have never heard any complaint with reference to the result of the operation of the statute in
[DOT]9907

question, upon that, the only occasion upon which it has been operated, except the [DOT]complaint which has come from the hon. gentleman himself. I am encouraged to think that there has not been any need felt of amendment to the provisions of this statute, from the circumstance that not only has no suggestion of amendment at any time come from any of the numerous judges who were concerned three years ago in working under this statute, nor has there been so far as I am able now to remember *any suggestion of amendment made by even the hon. gentleman (Mr. Boyce) himself.
No amendment has been proposed to this House during the sessions that we have had, and I have been gratified to think from that circumstance that this statute, which, as I have no doubt everybody who hears me is aware, I myself framed, has been found to answer well the purposes for which it was passed. In regard to the present situation, fortunately we are not in the same position that existed three years ago. No one, I presume, has any expectation that the general elections which follow upon a dissolution of this House, are any where in sight, or are at all liable to take place until there has been at least one session or perhaps two sessions more. In these circumstances there seems no danger to be apprehended that it may be found necessary on the part of the learned judges who are at present engaged in the preparation of these lists to curtail at all the time which the statute provides for taking the various steps.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can speak as one who suffered somewhat from the iniquitous lists that were gotten up by this government in 1908, perhaps more so than any other member of this House; in fact, so much so, that it was necessary for the Prime Minister or the Minister of Justice or the Secretary of State to send up eight or nine of the hel-meted gentlemen who stand around the corridors of this House, and other parts of this city, to protect life, and property during the voting period in the backwoods of Algoma. The manneT in which the lists were gotten up there ought to bring a blush of shame to the right hon. the premier, who now sits looking me in the face, when I tell him that there were 630 names placed on the voters' lists 50 miles from civilization, and placed under the control of followers of this government who controlled the camps where the men worked. One of the enumerators whom I questioned as to how he came to get so many names on the list, and as to whether he was satisfied that these men were still in the woods or were in the woods at all, said to me:	' I got
some of them from the foreman of the camp, some from a certain gentleman in

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext:
Blind RiveT, a lawyer who was very friendly to this government, and some from men in the woods who were coming out.' These men who were placed on the lists were hired in the city of Hull, in the city of Ottawa, and in different parts of the province of Quebec, and their names were placed on the lists the moment they set their foot in Blind River or between that and the place for the polling. They were so unacquainted with that part of Ontario that the gentleman who took their names from them was not able to understand one-half of them; so he took a jump at them, and those who were placed wrongfully on the lists had substitutes on polling day when they came to vote. 630 appeared at the polling booth, and 230 voted. The balance of the 630 refused to take the oath, because they were conscientious men after all; but that was no credit to the government, who placed their names on the lists. To show you that the lists were gotten up in a partisan spirit, under the hands of those friendly to the government, at the dictation I have no doubt of some of the members of the government, those men were^ practically placed in the position of criminals, and your humble servant was placed in a very peculiar position. When I or my agent objected to those names being placed on the list, I sent a subpoena to every man on the lists who I knew had no right to be there, and because I did not accompany it with conduct money, these men did not appear at the revision, and the judges allowed every name to re-main_ on the list. The result of the election in these bush polls was of course exactly what we expected. I had the magnificent number of 18 votes to my credit as against 200 or more to the credit of the gentleman who intended to have. their votes, and got them. As my hon. friend from West Algoma (Mr. Boyce) has said, there should be no curtailment of time in getting up the lists in the northern parts of Ontario at any rate. The distances are great. Although I live within a hundred miles of some of the points in my constituency, I have to travel 570 miles to get to those points. Moreover, a great many people do not see the proclamation at all, because they are scattered in hatches through the woods, while the proclamations are posted only where there are school houses or at other public places; so that in many parts of Algoma the men entitled to vote do not know that a proclamation has been issued, and that their names are on the lists until it is too late. Now we have a new condition of affairs in that district. There is now the district of Porcupine, with a great number of people there who were not there at the time of the last election.
I am told that there are some 10,000 people there. Then, we have the Grand

Trunk Pacific crossing the northern part of the district of Algoma, and that is hard to get at. So that it is necessary for this government to see that plenty of time is given, and that a careful list is made up in the northern parts of this province. I hope the government will not repeat what they did in 1908. I think it was a very unfair handicap. I am never afraid to go up against any reasonable proposition in an election, so much so that I have the honour, which perhaps no other member of this House has, of having won four general elections in six years. So that I am not any ways afraid where there is not such a handicap placed upon me as was the case in the last campaign. I was glad, however, that the good people who were entitled to vote knew what they were voting for, and placed me in this House. I hope the next time we shall not have the same handicap.

speechtext:
For a few moments I wish to refer to a matter which I brought before the House the other day, in connection with the principle of state ownership in competition with private ownership, in order to secure better treatment for the public.
I pointed out that in the province of Ontario, where there is state ownership now in regard to hydro-electric power, there is a great improvement, and I urged that by the same instrument a great improvement could be made in the telegraph and cable charges in this country, if we adopted state ownership. I also elicited from the Postmaster General the statement that state ownership was likely to obtain in the matter of telegraphs and especially in connection with cables, and that an understanding had been reached by the Postmaster General of England in association with the Postmaster General of this country to have state ownership, 'and, therefore, a reduction in the tolls. While I am referring to that I wish to say that I hope no agreement will be made by which, for a small reduction in the telegraph and cable tolls, the right of the state to intervene and to establish its own cables will be interfered with. No parliament should part with a sovereign
right of the state. That was done some years ago to the great disadvantage of the province of Ontario, when the Ross government gave a monopoly to three companies to develop power at the Niagara frontier, and bound the state that as long as that franchise existed the state would not interfere. This was a wrong. The state cannot part with a sovereign right in that manner, and if it does any other parliament can rescind the Act. The same thing could happen in connection with the telegraphs and cables, if the state agreed, tor a small reduction to postpone the experiment of state ownership.
Having said that, I wish to come to another practical point where state ownership will render great benefit to the people of this country. This is in connection with the post office and the parcel post. The people of this country are to-day paying exorbitant express charges. it is true the Railway Commission had undertaken to reduce them, but the process has been very slow, and the people of Canada are dissatisfied with the express rates obtaining in this country. While the express companies which are owned by the railway companies, are making an enormous profit out of their charges.
Just to show you what can be done in this matter, I may say that only the other day the Railway Commission of the United States intimated to the express companies that they proposed overhauling their rates. The result was that a great reduction has already taken place in express charges. It was not only the threat of the railway commission which reduced the rates in the United istates, but rather also the well known fact that there is a widespread agitation in that country to-day for the adoption of the parcel post system of England. We have in Canada a better parcel post system than they have in the United States, but our system is not as good as the English system. The effect of the English parcel post system-and in fact of the European parcel post system-because they have a better one in Germany-is to give the people an express service which does not cost one-third of the rate prevalent in Canada, and there is no such thing in England or Germany as the tyranny of the express companies so well known in America today.
Some centuries ago, the greatest departure in scientific subjects was when Sir Francis Bacon came forward with his great work in regard to scientific investigation. He said he had found a new instrument or new method in regard to scientific investigation, which he called the principle of induction. This brought about a revolution in scientific discoveries and in philosophy. Well, the great political principle to-day in regard to economics is state competition, as

against these great public service corporations.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Not good for reciprocity.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext:
I do not see the point of my hon. friend's remark. However, if we cannot have absolute public ownership in this country, we can at least have the state in competition with these companies. .1 have tried to show the other day that if the Intercolonial system were extended we would have a reduction in freight rates. This seems to me to be a self evident fact. To-day we have an organized parcel post system in this country which ought to be extended. The government is pledged not to extend it because the railway companies have told them they must not do so, using this pretense that if the parcel post rates are reduced the country storekeeper will be injured. There may be something in that, but it is a peculiar thing that every time 1 heard that argument, I was able to trace it back to the express companies. My contention is that all the people of Canada would be greatly benefited if the parcel post system of this country were extended and put on the same basis as the parcel post system of Great Britain, and still more if it were put on the basis of the parcel post system of Germany. Every citizen of this country feels the .burden of these express charges, and while the Railway Commission has not yet been able to catch up with them and effect a reduction, I think we oughr to go ahead and increase the weight of the parcels we allow to go through the parcel post. We ought to reduce the rates, and make them what they are in Great Britain or in Germany. If we do that a great benefit will be conferred on our people.
Just to show you that the railways dictate the policy in regard to these matters, I need only tell you what is admitted to be the case in the United States. It has been found that the railways control the express companies. The shareholders of the express companies are pretty well spread out, and have brought a great deal of influence to bear in arguing that the parcel post system cannot be adopted, much less extended. John Wanamaker, the late Rost-master General of the United States was asked While he was in office why the people of the United States could not have a parcel post system. He said there were four reasons, and the four reasons he gave were the names of the four great express companies operating in that country, every one of which is controlled by the railways. The railway lobby in the Senate of the United States has been all powerful for 20 years, and it is, apparently, all powerful yet. But the day of relief is at hand, and the widespread movement Mr MACLEAN.
in the United States for the adoption of a parcel post system, in connection witn the threat of the Interstate Railway Commission to reduce the rates, has brought about *& great reduction in the express charges in force.
Every time the attempt has been made it has been stopped by some great influence, and that influence comes from the railways. We are told that we were to have an international court in regard to railway matters. The chairman of our commission, and the chairman of the United States commission in consultation devised a scheme, and I believe it was authorized by law. But somebody has interfered, and it is a dead letter. My information is that the railways have been sufficiently powerful with the government to have the proposal tied up, and made innocuous so far as they are concerned. If these corporations can exert such an influence, if for twenty years they have been able to prevent the expansion of our parcels post, the people of this country ought to know it, esipecially In view of the fact that an election is near at hand. The people ought to have an opportunity to say whether we are to have the benefit of the parcel post system. It is all very well to have a skeleton of the system, but that is not enough; you must have life in it. The life is this principle of state competition with these corporations. Extend your parcel post system, and the express rates in Canada will be cut in two to-morrow. I would remind the House, of the experience I had in the Railway Committee some years ago. I took some action with a view to bringing the express companies within the purview of the Railway Act. We had a special committee on the subject of which Sir William Mulock was chairman. At our first meeting the express companies appeared by their lawyers, and presented the argument that they could not be brought under the Railway Act, because they carried parcels partly by water, and only partly by rail. That was argued for two days. When the lawyers were through, I said:	If that is
your argument it would be better for us to seek relief in an expansion of the parcel post system. The lawyer came back next day, and withdrew his whole argument, atj-mitting that the express companies could be brought within the operation of the Act. The railway companies which own the express companies feared the competition of a state-owned, state-operated parcel post system. Nothing would do so much to improve conditions in the west as to bring into operation the principle of which I have spoken. I challenge representatives of the west to say what they think of the efficacy of the parcel post system in reducing express charges. The competition of state-owned utilities with telegraphs, cables

and express would be a great relief to the people _ of the west. The proposition is self evident, and only needs to be applied. And the only reason I can find why the people of the west, and of Canada generally to-day are paying exorbitant express charges is that the expansion of our parcel post system has been checked. The fruit men of Ontario, time and time -again, have brought forward their grievances in connection with the transportation of their products. I may be told: The parcel j>ost system could not handle fruit. Whyj in Germany the post office handles all kinds of farm products. And it not only takes the farmers' products to town, but it markets the goods, and brings back the money, and the empty package to the farmer at night. And the farmers and florists, and other producers in England use the parcel post system in the same way. This system has been the gTeat instrument in the reduction of express charges. And if that is done in Europe, there is no reason why it -should not be done here. The system would be of great advantage to the farmers also in making purchases in the city, which purchases have to be carried over long distances. In the application of this principle that I advocate there is far more for the people than in this vaunted reciprocity. Give our people cheap transportation rates, and they will get better prices for their products. The return to the farmer is measured by the freight charge for the rule of the railway men is to charge all the traffic will bear. On the other hand, the state in competition with the railway that seeks to give the service at as low a rate as possible for the benefit of all. But here in Canada, and in America generally, which pretends to be the progressive part of the world is the most completely tied up to corporations. You cannot get for the people benefits that have been enjoyed by the people of Europe for fifty years past. It has been a surprise to me that not a single man from western Canada, so far as I know, has stood up in the House, and presented the high railway charges put upon the people of the west. I made a speech not long ago dealing with this question in connection with Canadian Pacific railway rates. There are members of the grain growers' organizations in the west who have defended their own rights. They have been in conference with the Prime Minister, and he has proposed to meet their grievances by giving reciprocity. I have had letters from some of these grain growers' associations, and one thing mentioned in these letters was the fact that when I ventilated the proposition not a single member from the west protested against the exorbitant and unfair charges of the railways. I contend that the relief to the people of the Canadian west is not
to be found in reciprocity, but in reduced railway charges. Do not you suppose that the Canadian Pacific railway could reduce its passenger rates, with the enormous travel they have on all their trains? They could easily give the people a two cent rate. But they will never do it until they are forced to do it. And a railway commission will never force them to do it, but state competition will bring it about in a single day. If my voice can reach the people of this country-and it may be difficult for me to make myself heard beyond this House-it will make known to the people this new political economic principle, and its effect in helping the development of the country, and affording relief to the people from unfair treatment by great and powerful corporations. That principle is the 'Competition of the state with these corporations. The state must either tie these corporations down or go into competition with them. We already have that principle applied in part. We have telegraph lines of our own, and we have a parcel post system. But these must be energized and made effective, and their tolls reduced. And somebody must be put in charge of the department who will realize that, as this is a great public department, public service is expected of it.
I give the Post Office Department credit for doing considerable service, for the people of Canada. There have been improvements, but the greatest improvements that can be made is to follow the lines of the post office department in European countries, and give us an efficacious parcel post system, a system that will meet the wants of the people. It won't hurt the railway companies. The right hon. gentleman and his friends say they believe in the doctrine of competition. Let us have competition, but don't let us have combination. There is combination now. The railways combine to keep up the rates, and they terrorize the government so that the government will not provide competition. Now, let us give the competition, and let it be a state competition if necessary. But let us have that competition, and a great benefit will accrue to the people of this country, a benefit that will not depend upon the whims of -another nation, but -upon the action of o-ur own government. It is for the state to -see that the people get fair and just treatment, and an excellent and cheap service. My object will be served if, in some way, the attention of this country can be drawn to this great new principle, that of state competition against corporations, which are exorbitant in their charges, which are -arrogant in their treatment of the public, and will only do their duty when they -are compelled to. Now, I trust the Postmaster General will have even more to say than he said the other day when he admitted that he was doing some-

thing to reduce the cable tolls, and that, perhaps, something -would be done to reduce telegraph tolls. But it is not promises we want, it is performances., The old Greek adage -was that to play upon the heart you must play upoq the heart, and the only way to bring the express companies to time is by establishing a parcel post system. If you do that we will then have, within one day, an improvement, we can out the express charges in this country in two. There is something that the government can do for the people of this nation.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext:
I am almost inclined to believe in telepathy, for I have been for several days working on <a plan to establish a parcel post system. I have been much interested of late in reading a very able series of articles published in ' McClure's Magazine ' of New York, and in one or two other magazines, on this very important question. In fact, my hon. friend probably knows that there is an editor in New York, a Mrs. Low, who for the past few years has made a special study of the application of a parcel post system- to the United States. In my hon. friend's statement there are many things with which I agree. The parcel post system in Europe, especially in England, France and Germany, has been a boon to the people of those countries. It is surprising what distance a parcel can be carried- at a cheap rate. When one compares the cost of carrying a parcel between Canada and Great Britain with the cost of carrying a parcel between Toronto and Halifax, one canciot but be surprised at the discrepancy between the charges. It costs -more money to send a parcel from one Canadian town to -another, -or from one province to- another, than it costs to send the same parcel across the Atlantic. You may ask why that is so. Wei, it is one of these things that can hardly be explained-. You may ask why a letter sent from Dover to Calais, from the shores of England to the shores of France, costs five cents, and a letter sent from Halifax to the Yukon, or to Melbourne, Australia, only costs two cents. That is one of the -secrets connected with the mail systems of the world. As I said, I have taken a great deal of interest in this question since I took office. My hon. friend will remember that about i906 or 1907, I made an announcement that the department was prep-arin-g a parcel post system for Canada. My hon. friend states that the old enemy is the railway corporations. I cannot say that it is the railway corporations. I supose my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) would be better informed than myself on that subject. But this singular fact occurred at the time I speak of. The moment the announcement was made that a policy could be Mr. MACLEAN.
shaped within twenty-four hours-because the Postmaster General has all the powers to start a parcel post system within a very short time with the legislation already upon the statute bo-ok in the Post Office Act- as I was saying, the -moment it was announced that we could readily establish a parcel post system in Canada, at once, for weeks and- for m-onths, the department was simply flooded with petitions again-st s-u-ch a system. These petitions -did not come from cities, but they were signed by farmers -and by country storekeepers, -and the argument which they used against the -establishment of that system was that the departmental stores would get all the benefits of the system. One peculiarity which struck me at the time was that all these petitions from every province were couched in the same terms, they were -all either printed or typewritten, and- the language was the same. There (is apparently an organization against the establishment of a parcel post. In my judgment a parcel po-st should benefit the farmers and benefit the outlying districts, and I was surprised to find these -objections coming from farming districts and from the storekeepers. On many -occasions I have tried to take up this question. I think that -a good preliminary to the -establishment of a parcel post system has -been the rural mail delivery. This, I may s-ay, is on -a fair way to success. I aim pleased to inform the House that this year, in the city of Toronto, we are manufacturing 100,000 boxes for the rural mail system. I am pleased to state that in many of the -most po-pulous counties of Ontario, -in some of the western provinces, and in some of -the eastern provinces, the system is expanding daily, the department is spending freely, and I believe intelligently in that direction.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext: Ha-s the minister, in connection with a parcel po-st system, considered what size -or weight of package he would send- through the mail?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext: This would require a detailed statement, which I am not -able to -give. I have some figures, and from the investigations which I have ordered, and which are now being made under the direction of Mr. Boss, of Toronto, -if the parcel po-st is established we would- have to provide for parcels of the same weight and dimension as those carried in Great Britain. I forget what are the weights -mentioned, but I can give that right away.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext: I would like to ask the Postmaster General if, in view of the fact that he is considering the possibility of instituting a parcel post, he has found it advisable to consider the question of increasing the size of the rural post boxes. They would not hold a pound of butter or of sugar. I think they cost about $2 apiece.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext: My hon. friend refers to what we call the King Edward or rural mail delivery box?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext:
It is a fair sized box. At all events it is only a matter of detail.
I would say, speaking in favour of the parcel post, that the Post Office Department has the whole machinery in its hands and can within a short time start a parcel post system better than the railway or express companies can, because the express companies only reach certain points, whereas the Post Office Department reaches the 15,000 post offices that are spread from one end of this country to the other.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext: That would depend on the size of the package.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext: Certainly. If we were to establish that system the railway companies would immediately apply for higher i ates. They are at present applying for higher rates.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext: What railway? Mr. LEMIEUX. All the railways.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext: Has the Canadian Pacific railway applied for higher rates?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext: All railways-even the Intercolonial railway. We are paying mail subsidies to the Intercolonial railway -the government railway. _ The state-owned railways are also looking after their own interests. We have more difficulties with my hon. friend the Minister of Railways in the way of rates than with the private corporations. But, the first question to be dealt with would be to fix the standard of rates, because, of course, the mail cars would 'not only be filled with the ordinary mail matter, but the parcel post would take up a considerable portion of the space. Therefore, you would at once have to face the issue whether the railway mail rates should have to be raised. That is one part of it.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext: Would the Postmaster General tell me whether the arrangement with the railway companies at present is by weight or lump sum?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext: On the basis of mileage. It is 4 and 8 cents a mile. We have some old contracts with the earlier railway companies under which we pay less than 4 cents when it is a baggage car service, but the standard rates to-day are 4 cents if we use baggage cars and 8 cents if we use the railway mail cars. In the United States it is on a weight basis, but they are going to change it. They have experienced very many difficulties in coming to a settlement. There was a commission in session in New York for several months composed of officials of the United States government conducting an investigation and they found that the Post Office Department of the United States had been mulcted by the railways since the establishment of the mail service.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext: Does the minister know what the arrangement is in Great Britain in respect of parcel post between the post office and the railways?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext: I could not give my hon. friend that information. I did not expect that this question would come up this afternoon, but, in Great Britain they have the telegraph, telephone and cables, and a most perfect system of parcel post. What special arrangements they have with the railway companies I could not say, but of course they pay subsidies as we do.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext: But they give a fine service.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext: A splendid service-the best in the world.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext: Let us try it.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext: But my hon. friend must not forget, and this must be credited to the post office system not only in Canada, but in the United States, that the conditions are very different. You can travel from London to Paris in less than a day, while here it would take more than a week to travel from one end of the country to the other. Therefore, that has always to be considered in the establishing of any such service. Several months ago, after the publication of those very able articles in the United States by people who have made a special study of this case, I gave Mr. Ross of Toronto, who is personally in favour of the parcel post system, _ authority to look around and consult with people, especially in Ontario, where I met, a few years ago, the strongest opposition, I am sorry to say, when this question was mooted for the first time. I have instructed him to investigate and prepare a report. I expect this report veTy shortly and then I will be able to say something more definite upon the question. I am glad that my hon. friend has brought this .question before the House this afternoon, in order to invite the attention of the country and the House to the consideration of this very important system.

speechtext:
I desire' to say a word in reference to the matter of excessive rates brought forward this afternoon by the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean). I do not know of anything to-day in Canada that is a greater handicap to the business of the country than the rates that are
(JOMMO.NS
charged by express companies. That applies more particularly to the north-western provinces than to any other part of Canada. I speak from experience because the concern of which I am president in my own town fills an express car every day with express parcels. Most of these parcels are small and they go to all parts of the country. During the fall of the year, the busy season, we probably ship to a greater extent than a car load a day. I find that the rates are most excessive. In the western Canadian provinces they are handicapped to such an extent that it is almost impossible for them to give <you repeat orders for goods to be shipped to them when they have to go by express. They have to give you large orders, buy once a year, and get their goods shipped by freight for the reason that if they repeat and have a parcel sent to them by express they are unable to pay the excessive freight charges. I know that in one case where I shipped a parcel, and not a very large one . either, to British Columbia, the express charges on it were $D0- over one-third of the entire value of the whole parcel. The result of it is, as I have already stated, that business is handicapped in the west and it is handicapped in the east too. because wholesale merchants and manufacturers in the east are unable to get these repeat orders that they should have on account of these exorbitant and extravagant express charges. A further handicap when you ship by express is that if you happen to ship from your own station by a Canadian express company to a point at which they have no office and the parcel is handed over to the American express company, they charge you double rates. Altogether the people are actually robbed by the express rates in this country. I do not know_ of anything to-day in Canada that needs investigation and looking into to such an extent as do the express rates. Two or three years ago there was an investigation into some of these express companies and the profits they were making were so exorbitant that one could hardly believe the figures when he read them. We have, as the hon. member for South York has stated, transferred to the Railway Commission power to regulate freight rates. I do not want to find any fault with the Railway Commission.
That Board has been doing good work and I think the people of Canada appreciate it, but, I cannot understand what is the trouble with them in connection with these express rates. It is two years since this matter went before them and there has not been a word from them in connection with it. Are they making any effort to relieve the people of this country from these exorbitant rates and charges; if they are, we know nothing about it. I am also interested in a line of business in the United Mr. LALOR.
States and the rates there are far different from what they are in Canada, because you can ship quite a parcel in the United States for ten cents, whereas in Canada there is no rate under 25 or 35 cents. The question of express rates in this country is of the greatest importance, and I hope the Railway Commission will move more expeditiously in the matter than they have done.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext: Is there in Haldimand county the same prejudice on the part of country store keepers against departmental stores as there is in other parts of Canada?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext: There is no doubt that the country merchants are very generally opposed to the parcel post system especially if large parcels are to be taken through the mails. The large departmental stores are a very great handicap to the country merchant, and it is very doubtful indeed whether they give the people much greater value than they get from the country stores. There is a strong inclination on the part of the people of the country to take a catalogue issued by one of these departmental stores and order something that is now sent to them by express, and if there was a parcel post system, it is very questionable whether this practice would not be carried on to an enormous extent to the detriment of the country merchants. The parcel post system is a debatable question, and it is possible that in the interests of the public generally, it might be carried too far.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext:
Of late years it has become so easy for great corporations to coalesce under the same management or arrive at an understanding with regard to rates that the public are often unfairly treated in the matter of charges for the use of these public facilities. This applies to railway companies, express companies, telephone companies, telegraph companies and others. It is universally admitted that :t is very difficult for parliament to interfere with these wealthy corporations for the protection of the people. So powerful are they and so far-reaching the influences they can bring to bear on governments that it is almost impossible to get any government with sufficient moral courage to grapple with them in the public interest. I was a member of a committee to inquire into certain rates charged by public utilities, of which Sir William Mulock was chairman. From every part of the country there were people coming to these corridors, lobbying the members, telling them what would happen to their political friends, what great injustice would be done these corporations, how the public would suffer, and bringing every influence to bear on the representatives of the people and of the

government to stop interference. It has been said over and over again that but for the influence brought to bear on the government at that time to frustrate the plans of Sir Wm. Mulock, that gentleman would not be on the bench to-day but would still be a minister of the Crown. They made it so disagreeable for him that he chose to leave public life rather than to submit to the indignities heaped upon him. I was a member of that committee and I know what difficulties1 .confronted him. In my judgment the solution is either independent competition which will afford reasonable charges, or otherwise absolute control of these utilities by parliament. Parliament must deal with that problem one way or the other. I believe the time has come when no government can remain in power that is not possessed of sufficient moral stamina to grapple with these problems. We have tried competition by subsidizing other lines of railway and granting other charters, but our experience is that when competition appears these interests get their heads together and come to an understanding for their own benefit and remove the competition we expected to get. We have in a measure tried control under the Eailway Commission which, although it does not come up to our full expectations, is certainly doing something. Perhaps it is not doing all we expected of it, because we have not given it greater powers.
Now, what has competition accomplished? Have we examples from sources that are not controlled by corporations to show whether it does good or not? I cited an example to this House many years ago which will bear repeating-the carriage of grain by a private-owned railway as compared with its carriage by the government-owned railway at a figure which the gov-vernment declared paid, but which thle private corporations have not been satisfied with as sufficient to enable them to pay their enormous dividends. The Canada Allantic railway, a private corporation, carried wheat, for instance, 346 miles for 2.27J cents, a little over 21 cents a bushel, while the government railway carried it 828 miles, nearly three times the distance, for the same charge. That was healthy competition. When that fact was brought out, the Minister of Railways was asked if it paid to carry the grain at that figure. The answer was that having regard to the return cargo it did pay. That is one concrete illustration among several that I could give which will serve to show the advantage of healthy competition. If the Intercolonial railway had been extended to Parry Harbour so that it could have taken the grain from there instead of receiving it at Montreal from the Grand Trunk railway, it could have hauled it from Parry Harbour to Halifax for very much less than 313
it cost to haul it jointly by the private-owned railway and the government-owned railway; and had the government railway been extended to the Georgian Bay, there is no doubt that the private-owned railway would have been obliged by the competition to reduce its rates. Let me give another example that came within my own experience a few years ago. I required to get a piece of machinery of only 400 or 500 weight from a firm between 30 and 40 miles east of Toronto. The charge for delivering that in Toronto was $5; yet a farmer offered to haul it with his team at the same price, although we did not give him any subsidy to help him to carry it, while we subsidized the railway very heavily. Then, I take the express charges. Farmers often have to get a small piece of machinery. I have had to do it more than once-a piece of machinery that cost me 25 cents, and I have paid 40 or 50 cents express to have it carried less than 50 miles. This is exorbitant and unfair, and there should be some authority in the land to see that justice is done to those who are compelled to use these public utilities. The same is the case with regard to the telephone and the telegraph system. I remember ordering a small article a part of a farming implement, through the telephone at a distance of less than a hundred miles. The article cost me 40 cents; and the express and telephone cost me $1.20. And that is called^ reasonable. I say it is little better than thievery, and so long as there is not some authority in the land to control these, public utilities, so long will these exorbitant charges continue. On one occasion in this House, when the government was being criticised for not controlling the railways in the interest of the farmers, the Hon. Edward Blake made this remark: 'I have often thought of it and have searched my brain to find some means of controlling them, but I have long since come to the conclusion that it cannot be done, for two reasons, that these corporations, when they do wrong, have no body to be whipped, and they have no soul to be damned.' Therefore they go on with evidently no fear of the future. If these corporations were not earning big dividends, it might be pleaded on their behalf that they were not making exorbitant charges; but -when you see the stock of the Canadian Pacific Railway selling up to between 200 and 300 per cent, you can take this as evidence that their earning powers and their returns from the subsidies which parliament gave them, are yielding them more than they are entitled to. So it is with the express companies. The glimpse which the railway commission has recently given the public of what these companies have been doing has shown that what they have been making out of the public has



been away out of proportion to what was required to pay a large dividend on every dollar they invested in the service. I join with the hon. member for South York every time in demanding that these public utilities should be brought under such control, if there is no possibility of having a healthy and permanent competition, as to secure for the people the service of these utilities at a moderate and reasonable cost.	_
The sooner parliament deals with it the better. Some may say it is a heavy task, but parliament is here for that purpose, and we should never shrink from any task that confronts us as parliamentarians or as a parliament. These problems are not impossible of solution if we apply ourselves to them, and until that is done I will be an advocate of government ownership of these utilities, or absolute control over them by some commission, power or authority which will force these corporations to do what they ought to do in the interests of the great users of these public utilities.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext:
I was not present when this discussion started, but I have heard enough from those who have spoken to understand that this is one of the most important matters which could possibly come before this parliament. Originally, I understand the question had to deal with parcel posts, but it seems to have extended a little beyond that, and taken in the express rates and freight rates.
If there is any part of this country of ours where this question is all important, it is the west. I do not intend to say very much about freight rates now, because, if I understand it, it is not the intention of the hon. gentleman who first brought up the question to have the matter dealt with now, but when the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) introduces legislation into this House to give a guarantee of $35,000,000 to the -Canadian Northern railway for a railway from Port Arthur east, and only gives $2,000,000 to build the Hudson bay railway, to use an expression far more forcible than elegant, I think that is simply rotten legislation, and had it not, been that we were about to have an election we would never have heard of such rotten legislation being introduced.
We have no parcel post in this country, so I do not know that there is very much use spending time discussing it, we have, however, express rates and freight rates which are very unsatisfactory. I would like to have an answer from some member of the government. I would ask the government if the present Railway Commission has full jurisdiction over the express rates of this country.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext:
Personally I have no doubt that the legislation now on the Mr. SPROULE.
statute-boks gives the Railway Commission full authority over the express rates in the Dominion of Canada, but it does not cover international express rates.

There is no question about the freight rates and express rates being too high, and I agree with any hon. gentleman who says in this House that it is the duty of this government to take the matter up. It is one of the most serious grievances of the west, and if the government had been as anxious to settle the grievances over which they have control as they have been in running to Washington, in an endeavour to do something which a great many people think is of no use, they would have been doing something for the benefit of the country. Through rates are not so bad. If you go west of Winnipeg and ship goods to Port Arthur or further east, you get practically the same rates as they have in the United States for similar distances. That being so, why should the western local express and freight rates be so high?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext:
I want to endorse very fully all that has been said by my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean), my hon friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner), and my hon. friend from Haldimand (Mr. Lalor) in Tegard to the overcharges in express and freight rates. Without desiring to take up the time of the House with a reiteration of the arguments which have been so far laid before us, I would like to place on record one instance of the way in which the public of western Canada-and probably the whole of Canada-are being robbed by the railway companies in freight rates. The railway companies of the west advertise that pedigreed live stock is carried at half rates. On the face of it this looks pretty well. It looks as though it were in the interest of the farmers and of agriculture. But when any one happens to send a pure-bred animal from one point to another, he finds that instead of paying half rates he is paying full rate, because of the method followed by the rail-wav company, which is to double the weight of the animal, and then cut the transportation rate in two.
I see that my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) smiles, but I happen to have in my pocket the proof of what I am saying. I have here a bill which I received myself last week, for freight on a thoroughbred stallion. If my hon. friend knows anything about thoroughbred driving horses even, he will know that there never was a driving horse

which weighed 4,000 pounds. Yet, that is the weight charged against me by the Canadian Northern railway. After figuring it out at 4,000 pounds, the transportation is cut in two. I think the government is blameworthy for this condition of affairs, because no man or company should have the right to charge more than the actual value of the transportation furnished. I think this is a matter that ought to be attended to at once by the hon. minister under whose control it comes.

speechtext:
This debate, Mr. Speaker, started with a discussion of the question of parcel post in Canada, and led up to a criticism of the express rates prevailing throughout the country.
There can be no question that the express charges are too high; I do not defend the express companies so far as that is concerned. But it must be remembered that they carry an immense variety of parcels. One has only to notice the express wagons as they go about the city to see that they carry many parcels that the post office would not want to carry. And I should think that the small parcels, such as the post office ought to carry would be the very ones the express companies would not want. And this small class of business must be expensive for the express companies. When a parcel is to be picked up, they must send a man with a horse and wagon perhaps many blocks distant from their office, and in the city of its destination, equal trouble must be taken in delivering that parcel. There must be a great deal of expense involved in this business, expense which, I think, many people are apt not to consider. I am not defending the rates of the express companies, 'but they, like other people, are entitled to fair play. An attempt is made to compare our conditions in this matter with those of England. But no such comparison can be made with fairness. You can cross England in a very few hours; it takes days to cross Canada. Our population is very much more scattered than theirs. So far as the matter under discussion is concerned, the two countries cannot be compared. I am quite in favour of the government taking any reasonable course to reduce express charges. The charges on parcels should be regulated_ by weight, and that is not done to-day. I had proof of that only recently. I sent a parcel on which I paid 75 cents. When it arrived at my home, the expressman wanted 45 cents. I am not complaining of the attempt to charge twice; that was a mistake; but the fact that the charge was different at the shipping point and at the receiving point for exactly the same parcel shows that they have no proper scale of charges. Especially such small parcels as are referred to by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) should be charged 313*
for weight. Of course, there are parcels, millinery goods and articles of that kind, that take up much room yet are very light. But, as a rule the charge should be strictly by weight. It would be better, in the case of most of these parcels to leave the business to the express company rather than to try to do the business through the post office. The express company gives a receipt for a package and undertakes to deliver the goods in good order. I do not know that the government would want to carry parcels on that basis. I have had some experience in this kind of business, and I believe that some people are harsh in their remarks about the work of the express companies.

I wish to refer briefly to a matter that I had occasion to mention yesterday, namely, the Chinese Investigation Commission at Vancouver. At the conclusion of my remarks I left it to the judgment of the House whether or not we should put on record our opinion as to the failure or the government to present that report. In consequence of the nature of the discussion which followed I thought it my duty to proceed further, so I gave notice to the government of my intention to move a resolution to-day expressing the opinion of this House that that report and the evidence should be laid on the table. I am happy to say that on this occasion the view of the government has come to coincide with my own. The fact that the first minister presented the report at the opening of the House to-day relieves me from my duty to proceed with the motion of which I have given notice. But, with the permission of the House I would like to refer very briefly to the suggestion of the first minister that I wasted time in occupying three hours in presenting what I did of the evidence, and commenting upon it. I would like to contrast that statement of the Prime Minister with the volume of evidence he has presented here to-day. I have not yet had the opportunity to look at that evidence and report, but I should think, from seeing it as it was laid on the table that it must cover in the vicinity of 10,000 pages. I think that if the government can find a person to make a readable summary of evidence so voluminous including a little comment, and do it in less than three hours, that person must oe a Jim Dandy indeed. In connection with the suggestion of wasting time, I believe it would be incumbent on some person to make a review of that report after its presentation. For my part, I should like very much to have made my summary from the official evidence, and also to have had the advantage of the conclusions ar-

rived at by the judge, so that I might apply his conclusions if he had forestalled me, and present the view that I thought best to present to the House. But, as I had not the official report, I was compelled to do the best I could and use the reports of the newspapers.
I	must express my disappointment at the suggestion made to-day that there will be no prosecution consequent on this investigation. From what I know of the evidence brought out I believe there are persons equally culpable with the few Chinese who have made their escape from the country since their complicity in these crimes has been brought to light. It seems to me that the detective force of the Dominion police could not be put to better use than in following up the inquiry started last summer, and so skilfully carried on, to run down the persons responsible for this conspiracy, to identify as many of them as possible, and to gather material upon which, I am quite sure, prosecutions could be sucess-fully conducted. I have not had the opportunity to read the report, but I should like to have been told by some person on the government side who has had that opportunity whether or not the commissioner makes any remark upon the patronage system, and the manner in which it is administered in Vancouver, and the irregularities resulting from it. To my mind that is the crux of the whole matter. If we could have assurance from the government that the patronage of the government at Vancouver could be taken out of the hands that now control it, better still, if we could have assurance that the customs appointments at Vancouver and elsewhere-because they are very important-would be relieved altogether from political pull, and put into the hands of the Civil Service Commissioners or some other independent authority, I think we should have some valuable assurance that frauds of this nature would not be so likely to occur in future.
Now, just a few words in conclusion with reference to my good friend the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman) the minister from British Columbia. A few weeks ago, that hon. gentleman took occasion to visit my riding. Because of the remarks' of the speaker who preceded him, and the other remarks of the speaker who came after him, this member of the government had no time to say anything of consequence at New Westminster except that he had not time to go into his subject, Yesterday in this House, though evidence was presented to show that he is regarded in some quarters-and not without show of reason- as particeps criminis in these frauds at Vancouver, to the extent at least of being an accessory after the fact toy exercising no diligence to secure punishment, again he had not time seemirgly, to make any reply Mr. TAYLOR (New Westminster).
or defence. It seems to me the minister from British Columbia is the most untimely man in this country-he never has time for anything.
I feel like apologizing to this House for the minister from British Columbia 1 wish to say that he is not a fair specimen of what we have out there. 1 thing that his prolonged and continuous residence at Ottawa must have deteriorated his quality, and that it would be a very good thing for the Minister of Inland Revenue if he could become again a permanent resident of British Columbia. I want to say to the House, what the minister from British Columbia knows very well, that the custom out there is when a man is attacked, to make some show of defence. He knows that even if Providence has not equipped us all with the same degree of manhood, that no matter what the inequalities may be between the attacker and the attacked, it is expected out there that when a man is told that he is put on his defence he should rise to the occasion and make some defence. Mr. Speaker, I think it is due to this House, and due to the government, and it is due to the minister himself, that we should have heard from him some explanation of the extraordinary course he is shown to have taken in connection with this Chinese investigation. I must express to you, Sir, and to the House my disappointment that the minister representing the province from which I come, should so utterly fail, in my estimation, to have regard for the duties, the responsibilities and the dignity of his office.
Sir WILFRID LAUR1FR. I think I can dispense my hon. colleague from taking any notice at all of the charges which have been made against his character, t think the silence of my hon. colleague, in the attack which has been made against him, is quite justified by the report which has been laid to-day on the table of the House. With regard to the action to be taken by the government on this question, I have not said that no prosecution should be taken, nothing of the kind. But 1 have not yet seen any others, not having read the report minutely. With regard to the insinuation of the appointment in the

custom house of men who are not fitted. I have only to say to the hon. gentleman, and he knows it-at all events he ought to know it-that the only party employed in the customs who has been suspected of anything wrong, is not an appointment of this government, but is an old officer who was appointed by our predecessors. No other man, so far as I know, has been charged by the commissioner or anybody else in the Customs Department, except the Chinese interpreter and the collector of customs. Of the only two parties who have been suspected of 'anything wrong, one is a fugitive from justice now and the other was not an appointee of this government.
