But the Prime Minister did not touch one very important phase of the situation. The commissioner, in his report, said the collector of customs had had duties imposed on him in connection with Chinese immigration which, added to his duties as collector of customs, made impossible demands upon his time. But he went on to say something more. He pointed out the nature of the administration of this Chinese immigration law at Vancouver, and he said that in many respects the administration of that law had been absolutely farcical. He pointed out the reasons why. The Prime Minister has not alluded to these, nor has he shown in what respect the government have taken any steps to make that which was farcical really effective. We do not know up to the present time, so far as I am aware, in what respect the administration has been changed in that regard. I am not suggesting that it has not been changed, it may have been; but up to the present time we have no information before us whatever on this subject. I think information should be given, if not to-day at the earliest moment possible, as to how matters are at the present time with regard to that question. Then there is another matter upon which I would like to have some information, that is about what time did this inquiry end, at what time did the taking of evidence cease; how long after, or was it before this report was made and received by
the government, and what steps, if any, have been taken since the receipt of the report in connection with any of these matters. It is said that the men who were indicated as guilty by the report have escaped from the country. When did the evidence disclose to the government that these men were in all probability guilty of some criminal act, and what is the reason they were allowed to escape after that evidence had been brought to the attention of the commissioners? These are all matters on which it is only reasonable that parliament should have some information. I do not know that the Prime Minister will be able to give it to-day, but I think he ought to give it on Monday, at the latest.

speechtext:
Before you leave the Chair I would like to refer for a few moments to the subject that was brought up by the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean). This subject of express rates is a very burning topic amongst the community at large, amongst the mercantile classes and amongst the farmers. I am pleased that it has been brQught before the House, and that the discussion has thrown some additional light upon the future policy of the government. It is quite true that there is a division of views on this subject, there is a divergence of opinion as to whether the adoption of a parcel post system would be of benefit to the country as a whole or not. The arguments advanced, as already stated, are that if a parcel post system is instituted, the large departmental stores will benefit at the expense of the country storekeepers. Now that is a very important matter, because these catalogue houses and these departmental stores are now competing very strongly with the storekeepers. I do not suppose that, in the matter of price or quality, these departmental stores are actually competing with the country stores.
But the fact that they advertise so extensively all over the country gives them an unfair advantage over the local trader with the result that the people of the country send their money to the larger centres, such as Toronto, and get inferior goods to those which they could buy at home for less money. Nothing that could be said in this House or out of it could make any headway against the immense volume of advertising that these departmental stores indulge in. The great campaigns of advertising which they conduct invariably lead to the conclusion in the minds of the public that prices .are lower in these departmental stores than they are in the home stores. When the discussion was at its height, when this question was at its hottest stage and before it was turned over to the Railway Commission, the fact was apparent to

everybody that the departmental stores were obtaining much cheaper rates of express on their parcels than the average public could obtain. We will take an express parcel. shipped by a departmental store a distance of 100 miles; the rate would be, say, 15 cents. Putting it in the reverse position the merchant or farmer shipping articles from an outside station back to the city would pay an express rate of 35 cents on the same weight of goods, so that there was a gross injustice done to the public in that way.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext: Do I understand my hon. friend to say that express companies discriminate in favour of departmental stores and against the public?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-VOTERS' LISTS IN UNORGANIZED DISTRICTS.
speechtext:
They did that extensively, and I have no knowledge that the commission has put in force rules against it. So much did they discriminate and so low were the express rates that were quoted to these departmental store people that I doubt very much whether this government could afford to carry goods by parcel post at such low rates. The public at large, and more especially the public who live in the cities, are very deeply interested in cheaper rates by express companies. Most of the articles that are consumed in the city-eggs, butter and other [DOT]country produce-are articles that pay express rates. These goods are shipped to the city by express for the simple reason that if they were shipped by freight the time occupied in their carriage would be so great that, being perishable, they would be destroyed. I know that one small town in my riding sends an average of one car by express every week of farmers' produce to the city of Toronto and the express rates would be very exorbitant on that. I have no doubt that one of the chief reasons why the people in cities pay such exhoitoi-tant prices for the food they eat to-day is the terribly high express rates which the farmers and dealers have to pay on the farm produce which they ship to Toronto and various other cities. I am told that fruit can toe shipped by express in cold storage from California and other distant points in the United States to the great centres in Canada at a much lower rate than would be charged upon same articles procured 25 or 30 miles out of the city. A basket of cherries or case of peaches could be brought from California at almost as low a rate of express as that at which they could be brought from Grimsby or Oakville.
This question has been discussed pro and con and there has been a great deal of agitation amongst the public with regard to it. As already stated by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Campbell) and others who have spoken, the question of freight on express rates is a burning one all over Mr. CURRIE (Simcoe),
the country. During the past winter the Manitoba 'Free Dress' devoted a great deal of time and space to quoting figures in order to show that in western Canada the rates of freight were far greater than the rates charged in the adjoining states of the Union. In that discussion the 'Free Press' took occasion to comment on some remarks that I had made in this House on a previous occasion. I wish to make a reply to the discussion of the 'Free Press' as far as freight rates in the West are concerned. This discussion of freight rates by the Manitoba 'Free Press' would have some point and would be of some value to this House and benefit to the country had the figures which they gave in their comparison with reference to the state of Minnesota not been open to question. What do I mean by that? I mean that about four years ago the state of Minnesota established a board to govern freight rates. This board was to have absolute jurisdiction over all the freight and railway rates within the state of Minnesota. The board was of a socialistic character. It held its meetings and it issued a schedule by which it cut freight rates then paid throughout the state in two. The freight rates that were paid and had been paid in that state until recently were such that they were fully 50 per cent less than the freight rates paid throughout the Canadian Northwest. To carry on the agitation in the west in regard to these freight rates emissaries were sent to Canada and copies of the schedule published by the Minnesota board were sent broad-past all over the Canadian Northwest. The railways in Minnesota brought this question before the courts .with a view of determining whether this board had acted properly and whether its jurisdiction were such that it could make this enormous, arbitrary cut in the freight rates. The railways succeeded in showing the court that the rates established by this board were absolutely wrong, that they were virtually confiscatory in their nature, inasmuch as it was impossible for the railways to carry freight for the rates that this revolutionary board had established there. The courts have given a decision against the. state of Minnesota and its board in that respect and, as I say, the arguments advanced by the 'Free Press' in using this comparison of freight rates between Minnesota and Canada are not trustworthy and of no value.
However, it is apparent to any person that in many cases freight rates, even in Ontario, are very unjust and wrong. My hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) referred to some freight rates within his knowledge. I could have said to him that the principal town in my Tiding, Colling-wood, is 35 miles from his principal town,

Markdale, and I can ship freight by wagon from Ooliingwood to Markdale at a cheaper rate than I can ship the same freight by rail.	*
The reason is that where there is interchange of traffic each railway charges its local rate thus making the through rate exorbitant. It is time for us to consider means to compel railways to interchange traffic in the interests of the people. The consuming public are deeply interested in express rates and the government of the day should be up and doing to provide a remedy for the existing evil. There are three lines of action possible; one, government control over the rates, a principle we have accepted by the appointment of the Railway Commission and another, the establishment of competition by the government. I may belong to an antiquated school, but to my mind, I consider it wrong for government to take any action which would unduly destroy private investment and enterprise. The Minister of Railways (told us, speaking on the Grand Trunk Pacific Bill, that we are no longer pioneers in Canada, but that the object of the government in assisting railway building in the west was to bring about competition. Our experience, however, is that when you bonus a railway to bring about competition you are simply doubling the charge on the public without attaining your object, for the railways get together and combine on rates to their own advantage. Can any one here say that when a new railway is brought into a town, genuine competition ensues. The only advantage a new railway affords the manufacturer is to save the expense of shipping over two lines, for, if he has only the Grand Trunk he can only ship over the Grand Trunk at carload rates, whereas if the Canadian Pacific railway comes to his factory he can ship to Canadian Pacific railway points also at carload rates. If the government compels railways.to exchange traffic, one railway will afford the same facilities as two will; the cost of the extra Tailway will be saved and in the end the public would get cheaper rates than they could by such so-called competition as I have spoken of. When we are talking of railway matters we are prone to think that the United States and Canada are the only two countries in the world, but let me point out what France has done. After the great war the government of France realized that they had to take steps to reorganize agriculture and other industries and that the best way to do so was to encourage the building of railways and canals. The government of France grappled with the question and spent enormous sums of money and the following citation from the Cambridge Modern History, Vol. XII, ' The Latest Age ' p. 101, will show what France did in respect of transportation matters:
In the matter of manufactures and commerce, the resources of the state were especially, and at this period lavishly, employed in creating for the nation a material equipment, which had been left in a singularly inadequate condition by the Second Empire, occupied as it had been with other matters. Credit is due to France that, immediately after her disasters, she did not shrink from this increase of burdens, but reasoned that by this means alone she could be enabled to liquidate the claims of her onerous debt. From this period dates the creation of roads and highways with such ramifications into country districts that the strivings of the new life from that time onward touched the tiniest villages and hamlets. The extent of the new roadways has been estimated at 200,000 kilometres, and at 1,200 millions tbe grants given since 1876 for this network; 120 millions are required for its annual upkeep. It has completed the great national and departmental highways, temporarily sacrificed to the need of railways, and since restored to high honour.
The time has come when in Canada we should consider whether the government ought not to direct its attention to co-ordination and co-operation such as the French people have brought about and which, to my mind is the only real method by which we will' 'ever secure lower freight rates.
We shall never have lower freight rates in. the west if we go on building transcontinental railways at the price we are doing. It is well known that the Canadian Pacific railway and the Canadian Northern railway would have lowered their rates if it had not cost so much to build the transcontinental line. The great need of the west is not so much through lines as branch lines. The railway companies and other land companies have taken the bulk of the lands near the railway lines. You will find very few people living within three or four miles of the railways in the Northwest. The bulk of the farming population [DOT]-the homesteaders-live eight or ten miles from the railways, some fifteen, twenty or thirty miles. These people expect and are entitled to railways, and the policy of parliament should be to build branch lines in the west, so that nobody would be obliged to haul his goods more than three or four miles to or from a railroad. Consider the ease of the island of Prince Edward. That island is endowed by nature with everything necessary to make it a great and prosperous farming country, hut it lacks transportation facilities. There is a government railroad running from one end of the island to the other. For many years, as long as I can remember, a tunnel has been advocated to offer the island closer connection with the mainland and _ the rest of Canada. I agree that that is a matter which should receive our earnest attention; but no engineer in Canada will say that that tunnel could be completed withing less than five or six years. But in the meantime the island is suffering for transporta-

tion facilities, acid the government has not devised a practical plan for giving it immediate relief. How could it be done? The island Tailway is a narrow gauge railway. If the government would provide a landing place such as we have at Point Tupper in Cape Breton, and change the gauge of the island railway so that the people could move their produce in car-loads by oar ferries direct to the mainland, the result would mean thousands of dollars saved to the people of Prince Edward Island every year. Yet neither the Minister of Raii-ways nor anybody else in the government has offered any practical suggestion. At present everything that leaves the island or goes to it has to be handled two or three times at great cost. Some hon. members cannot understand why freight rates are greater for short distances than for long distances. It is because the railways have to do much more loading and unloading of the goods for the short distances thaa for long distances. To return to the question of express rates, there is a third method by which those rates can be reduced, that is, by the government buying out all the companies that control the express business of this country and nationalize the whole system. If they are -allowed to go on as at present they may go- on watering their stock by capitalizing their earnings until the government will have to pay a vast su-m for them. The only fair and just method of dealing with them would be to nationalize these express -companies at a fair and reasonable figure, and proceed to carry on the express business of the country on a just and equitable basis. Then we would have no more discriminatory rates and no more rebates to large concerns like departmental stores, but we would have fair -and- equal justice to everybody, and the man who would benefit most would be the farmer who produces truck and small produce for the cities. The store keeper would also benefit, because he would get his goods cheaper, having t-o pay smaller rates for shipping them. I a-m very pleased that the -h-on. member for South York has -brought this matter before the House. I know that he would be the last man to suggest that the money -spent properly for the cars, the offices and buildings, the equipment and the development of the business -of the express companies should be either confiscated -or subjected- to unjust, unfair or arbitray competition. The most reasonable course would be for the government to establish a system whereby all the express (business of the country would be done in connection with the postoffice service. I trust that this question will again come before this House at a time when we can discuss it at greater length, and when we can put our views on record by having a resolution of the House on the question.

The subject on which I intended to address you to-night, Mr. Speaker, had reference to postal rates, and I would have preferred- not to take up the matter until the Postmaster General was- in his seat. However, he can read my remarks in ' Hansard,' and probably be in a position to answer them.
I did not intend to make any reference to matters which were discussed this afternoon-more -especially the question of express rates. I would rather leave that in the hands of gentlemen who are more familiar with the subject, and who have more to do with the express companies than I have. Not being in the business, I confess that I do not come in direct contact with the express companies, therefore, any grievances I might put forward would simply be of a secondhand nature.
A great deal has been said during the past year with reference to the excessive charges of the express companies. Whether the companies have undertaken to reduce these charges -or not is a point- upon which I am not informed. Some of the hon. members spoke this afternoon with reference to certain advantages which the departmental stores of Toronto, for example, would receive on account -of changes suggested in regard to the parcel post system, and of the advantages which they might also have under th-e express regulations. No doubt these departmental stores have very great advantages in the country. I think they _ secure these advantages by their peculiar mode of advertising-for instance, they will advertise that a certain article' which sold for $2 yesterday will be offered for $1 to-day, o-r that an article which was worth $1.50 yesterday can be had to-day for 50 cents. There are a great many people in the country foolish enough to believe these statements, hence the business done by these concerns.
I am glad the Postmaster General has come in, because this is something which will appeal to him directly.

These departmental stores send their catalogues from one end of the Dominion' to the other-you find them all over the country from Cape Breton to British Columbia. I was going to complain of the advantages which these companies enjoy in postal rates over other people or companies who do not do as large a business. Now I do not consider it fair that these departmental stores should have special privileges under the post office system- that is, that they should get a cheaper rate of postage than anybody else sending out a smaller number of catalogues, for instance. I remember within the last two years applying to the hon. the Postmaster General to get a like privilege for a constituent of mine; a man who was engaged in the manufacture of a spraying compound, and who was anxious to advertise it throughout the country, if he could get the facilities for sending his catalogues out at the same rates as ether concerns doing a larger business. I discovered then that the departmental stores in Toronto, which were doing a very large business, were able to send their catalogues at a lower rate of postage than a man in my county, simply for the reason that he did not send out such large quantities.
I	had always thought that there was no discrimination in postal matters, but that the man w'ho sent out ten letters a day sent them at the same rate as the man who sent out one hundred. But it would seem that the man who sends out a large number of catalogues makes a special rate with the Post Office Department, and thereby gets an advantage in the way of advertising over the man who does not do so large a business. If I am wrong in my statement, I hope the Postmaster General will put me right, for, as the matter is now understood it is a grievance in a part of my county. An industry is being carried there in a material for spraying fruit trees, known as the lime-sulphur mixture. If this industry could advertise as cheaply as others do, it would be of great benefit. I think the Postmaster General might take into consideration the smaller concerns _ of the country, and put them on a par with the larger concerns.

I would refer my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) to section 70 of the postal regulations, which reads:
Tlie articles of printed and miscellaneous matter comprised in the following list are subject to the rate of one cent for each two ounces or fraction thereof.
And included in this list are catalogues. I will read what my hon. friend has said, and will inquire if there is discrimination against the industry he has mentioned. I cannot find authority for it under the law. But I will inquire into the matter.

If I may be permitted, I would remind the Postmaster General that when I applied to him to get a special rate which, it was understood, was applicable to the large department stores in Toronto, the reason he gave me why it could not be given in that case was that the business was not sufficiently large to pay for the extra service that would be required where the catalogues were posted.
I have not read the regulations, and have no doubt they are exactly as the Postmaster General has read them. But it seems to me, after what I learned at that time from the Postmaster General that the regulations are not being carried out.
I will look into the matter.

The very extreme importance of this measure will amply justify, if any apology be needed, lengthy debates of the subject by the opposition as a whole or by individual members. The more this pact is investigated the more it seems to me, the matter calls for very grave consideration on the part of members of this House, and of the people at large. And the greater the opportunity the public has to investigate^ it the more the people justify the discussion by the very intelligent way in which they are now receiving the information that is being supplied them by members of this House, by the, press and otherwise. The measure is not only of very great economic consequence, but it involves very grave considerations, political and national. In fact, so grave, in my opinion, aTe the objections to this pact from the political and national standpoint that it may be said really to affect fundamentally the very constitution under which we live, the underlying principles of confederation. None of us need be reminded of our country's early history, and the many struggles of our people for constitutional government, and for economic, and political consolidation. These things are a part of Canada's recorded history. The changes I have referred to culminated, as we know, in the compact of the provinces which now forms our constitution, the Act known as the British North America Act. It does seem to me that that Act was framed not only for the consolidation, and advancement of Canada, but also to assist in the consolidation and advancement of the Britsh Empire. If proof of this were needed, we find it in the very words of the preamble of the Confederation Act itself. It says:

And whereas such a union would conduce to the welfare of the provinces and promote the interests of the British Empire.
That being one of the objects, we in our day and generation should see to it that nothing is done that shall alter our position or undermine British institutions or our imperial relation. For it seems clear that anything that undermines our British institutions or our British connection strikes a blow at Canadian nationality. I think a reference of this kind is not inappropriate having regard to the importance of this pact. The very terms of confederation seem to have been based upon the idea that the provinces then separated desided to trade together, and to combine into a federal union for the purposes of common defence, progress and advancement as well as for the promotion of their various provincial enterprises. Section 121 of the Bri-ish North America Act shows that the framers of the Act had this in view:
All articles of growth, produce, or manufacture of any one of the provinces, shall, from and after the union be admitted free into each of the other provinces.
Every hon. member is familiar with that section and I would ask them that it be viewed in that aspect. The provinces said: We are to trade together, there are to be no tariff walls between us, we stand back to back, and face the rest of the world.
As between us there is to be no tariff wall, everything is to be free that comes and goes between us; but we are to hold ourselves at liberty to shut out the rest of the world if so desired. Now that seems to have been a fundamental principle of confederation, and I do think that the extreme haste with which this government proposes to railroad this pact through the House without consulting the people is inexpedient and almost indecent, in face of the_ fact that there was ample time in which to have consulted the people. The provinces were not consulted as provinces; the people who are citizens of the various provinces were not consulted Therefore I say that what has been called obstruction bv the opposition is justified, and the opposition have done nothing more than their bare duty in that respect. This proposed change, in the opinion of many, is of such importance as to justifiy more than the hasty consideration which it received when it was brought into this House, ana was entitled to very full consideration on the part of the public at large. As I said a moment ago, the more this pact is considered the more apparent becomes the fact that the people regard it as a fundamental change. . Their existence in many respects is proposed to be altered by it, and we are face to face with a new condition which may in time bring about a new nationality. Now it would seem to me Mr. MACDONELL.
that the very fullest consideration should be given to this question. The Minister of Finance, when he brought this measure down, brought it down hastily, as he himself, I think, admitted in a speech which he delivered in Windsor Hall, Montreal; he admitted that there was not adequate information before the people of this country on which to form their opinion. I will read the quotation later from his speech on that occasion. What information the people have received they have otbained, in great measure, from the members of the opposition in this House, aided by their friends and allies throughout Canada. Because in this great fight the opposition have made allies. History appears to be repeating itself, events are similar to those that occured in 1878. Men are breaking from their old party affiliations, and many of them are allying themselves with the party that is opposing this pact. They are men who formerly opposed this party, and so we find various organizations growing up from day to day in this country, all in opposition to this pact.
Now we are told that there is an invisible border line extending some three thousand miles across this continent. Well, one does not like to be reminiscent in certain matters, but that line is not an invisible line. It was not an invisible line when many of the founders and forefathers of this country came across that line long years ago, and left behind them all their earthly possessions in the then republic. That line is still there, it is a line of national demarcation,. Tariff walls would not alter it if they were removed. The line is just as indelible now as it was then. I am not referring to that line with any hard feelings, nor do I desire to arouse any such feelings. But I say that the people who left that country long ago and came here to live under British institutions, which were guaranteed to them by thd British government, have a right still to appeal to that guarantee. On the part of the people of this country there is a strong desire to continue those British institutions and political affiliations with Great Britain. Now of course we are living in a utilitarian age. We are not dealing now with flag waving incidents, b( cause it is to be hoped that the hundred years of peace which has prevailed between ourselves and our neighbours to the south will soon be celebrated and will be repeated in the ages to come.
We oppose this pact both upon political and economic grounds. It does seem to me that, both from a political and an economic standpoint, it deserves more careful consideration than has been given it. It seems to me that the opposition to this treaty has made many friends and allies during the time it has been up for discussion. Many people have been

touched in their sentiments of nationality by its provisions. It was not thought perhaps by those who introduced it that it would have any sentimental aspect, or that it would be viewed from a sentimental point of view by the people of this country. But I can assure the hon. gentleman who introduced it that there are a great many people in this country who are opposed to it in their most sacred and patriotic sensibilities. They are opposing it because they believe it is calculated to endanger the political conditions under which they now live, is calculated to lead to profound changes in our commercial and political relations, and ultimately to political union with our neighbours to the south. There is that element who are opposed to it. Then we have the people whose interests are affected, people who view it from an economic standpoint, the great commercial interests of this country. It does seem to me that the great commercial and business interests of this country from end to end are opposed to this pact, men who have never taken any strong part in party politics in this country, or no part at all. One of the outcomes of this feeling is the Canadian National League, which has been recently formed with headquarters in the city of Toronto. It has been _ organized by a number of patriotic citizens who have inscribed upon the front of their literature their views and their reasons. These are men who, in private life and in business life, have not heretofore taken a prominent part in politics, and who have no notion of participating in public affairs, men who are not concerned which party is in power. These men have leagued themselves together to form this alliance. Permit me to read some of the objects of the Canadian National League:
The Canadian National League_ was formed following the protest against ' Reciprocity with the United States of America/ which was signed by eighteen supporters in Toronto of the Liberal party in Canada and published m the press on February 20, 1911.
The objects of the League are:
To oppose the adoption of the proposed reel-procity agreement Detween Canada and the United States of America, and to support such measures as will uphold Canadian nationality and British connection, will preserve our fiscal independence and will continue to develop onr present national policy of interprovimcal and external trade, under which the Dominion has achieved its present prosperity.
The basis upon which the League has been formed is Canadian nationality, British connection and fiscal independence.
Now surely no intelligent Canadian can quarrel with the objects of this League Canadian nationality, British connection and fiscal independence. These gentlemen have given numerous and weignty reasons in support of each and every one
of these objects. Hon. gentlemen in this House are well aware of the formation of this League, and of the high character of the men composing it, and of their aims and aspirations. These men have no purposes to serve but the public good. They honestly belive in the necessity of such an organization, because they believe that Canadian nationality, British connection and fiscal independence are more or less menaced by this pact. Now we have heard a good deal about the city of Toronto in connection with this question. We know that the Toronto Board of Trade went on record against this pact by a vote of something like 280 to 13. I desire shortly to read an extract from the address which Mr. Gage, president of the Toronto Board of Trade, delievered on the 19th of January of the present year.
Canada lias never known a time of such universal prosperity. Our farmers are prosperous, our merchants and manufacturers are prosperous, our labouring classes have abundant employment with good wages. Is it not a good time to leave well enough alone.
If our American friends wish t;o share m our unequalled prosperity, let their manufacturers continue to do as they have been doing in the past few years-locate branch factories in Canada-they will he welcome. If our American farmer wishes to 'get rich quick, let him follow the well-beaten trail made by nearly a quarter of a million farmers from the United States, who have already found homes in the Canadian west.
Surely no one can quarrel with that. It is believed by the board of trade, as indicated by the president's language which I have read, and by the members' vote which I have mentioned, that if this pact passes there will be a discontinuance of the Americans coming to Canada with their money and establishing manufactores or branches of their large American industries, 'these are not idle words, they are not words said in jest, or said simply for the purpose of making conversation; they are words uttered because it is believed that they are true. These are the business men of the community. They do not confine their remarks simply to the manufacturing element, but they refer to the farming community and point out how, if the American farmer wishes to come here, he can do so. Let me give the counterpart of that reference which I have read. I desire _ to quote Senator Beveridge from the American point of view upon the same aspect of the question. We all know of Senator Beveridge. On the discussion of this reciprocity measure, he spoke as follows:
There must he reciprocity with Canada. Our tariff with the rest of the world does not apply to our northern neighbours. That policy already has driven American manufacturers across" tile Canadian borders, built vast plants with American capital on Canadian soil, em-

I think not, but at all events this resolution of Congress was passed at a moment when reciprocity was in the air and it was passed in consequence of the repeal of the reciprocity treaty at that time. Although, Canada met with certain temporary losses by the cancellation of this treaty, the American people were apparently unaware of the fact that we were able to take care of ourselves, and indeed, the very next year, we began to show signs of our ability to be able to do without reciprocity in the future. We know what our friend, Mr. Champ. Clark
has said that we would joyfully become part of the republic and this and other similar expressions are used by American statesmen when referring to this pact, which at least shows what is in their minds when entering into the arrangement. In a recent speech in New-York, President Taft used this language:
I have said that this was a critical time in the solution of the question of reciprocity. It is critical because unless it is now decided favourably to reciprocity, it is exceedingly probable that no such opportunity will ever again come to the United States. The forces which are at work in England and in Canada to separate her by a Chinese wall from the United States, and to make her part of an imperial commercial band reaching from England around the world to England again by a system of preferential tariffs, will derive an impetus from the rejection of this treaty, and if we would have reciprocity, with all the advantages that I have described, and that I earnestly and sincerely believe will follow its adoption, we must take it now, or give it up for ever.
Such views are being constantly expressed by statesmen of the United States and circulated through their press. We know that Sir George Ross has declared it to be bis belief that annexation lurks at the bottom of this pact in the mind of our American friends. As confirmation of his opinion I cite this language of the Hon. G. S. Boutwell, President Grant's Secretary of the Treasury, and a member of Congress at the time of the repeal of the reciprocity treaty:

The fact of the annexation of Canada to the United States whether the event shall occur in a time near or remote, depends probably upon our action on reciprocity. Canada needs our markets and our facilities for ocean transportation, and as long as these advantages are denied to her, she can never attain to a high degree of prosperity. The body of farmers, labourers, and trading people will favour annexation ultimately should the policy of nonintercourse be adhered to on our part, and they will outnumber the office holding class, and thus the union of the two countries will be secured.
We were told then that the repeal of the treaty was to drive us into annexation, and that such was the policy of the Americans, but it failed in its aim. The Minister of Finance in introducing this measure referred at length to the connection of Conservative leaders in times past with reciprocity, but he touched very gingerly the period from 1838 to 1891, because he knows the state of public opinion in Canada on reciprocity during that period. He knows that the defeat of the Liberal party in 1891, was largely due to its advocacy of that policy. We know that prior to 1891 Mr. Erastus Wyman was busy with his friends

in New York, Mr. Carnegie and others, and he was helped by his friends in this country, Mr. Tarte and Mr. Merrier, the ' political allies of the Liberal party. We .know the course taken at that time by the Hon. Edward Blake, and that he and Gold-win Smith declined to follow in the footsteps of these men who wanted to lead us into commercial union. The Minister of Finance said very little about that period.
The hon. Minister of Finance is on record on many occasions in regard to the Imperial preference, >and we are now fed with preference pap, so to speak. When complaint is made of this reciprocity pact, the public is told: 'See what we have done for England; see the British preference.' Well, the British preference is going to become non-existent if this pact passes; there will be very little of it left. On the items enumerated in the schedule to this pact the preference will be zero, because the duty the American people will have to pay on them when they come to this country will be nil. At the time the Minister of Finance intnoduced the preference, there "was no intention on his part or on the part of the government to give a preference to Britain alone. We are told now with great acclaim that the Liberal party gave the British preference. No one knows better than the Finance Minister that at that time it was a preference not to England alone, but to any nation that could qualify by giving us as favourable treatment as we gave it. When the Finance Minister introduced the preference in 1897, at page 1111 of 'Hansard,' he said this:
I stated that the tariff that I am about to read to you is the general tariff, but that before I conclude I shall be prepared to make a statement in relation to a special tariff that will apply to Great Britain and any other country which is prepared to accept the conditions which that tariff imposes.
Later on he spoke as follows, page 1131:
We do not by our resolutions offer anything to Great Britain alone. We recognize the fact that Great Britain by her liberal policy is in a position to avail herself of this offer immediately, hut we make our offer not to Great Britain only, but to every nation which is prepared to accept it. We make it to every country which is willing to establish fair and reasonable trade relations with Canada.
On the same page, speaking of the favoured nation treaties, he spoke as follows:
I say that it does not seem fair and reasonable that we should he obliged, while we are offering certain terms, not to Great Britain only but to all countries which will place themselves in the same position-it does not seem to be fair and reasonable that we should be obliged to extend the privileges of this schedule, which we call a reciprocal tariff, to nations which are not willing to do anything in return.
Now, I have just two comments to make on that statement. One is that the offer Mr. MACDONELL.
was not made to Great Britain alone; it was made to any country that chose to accept it. Secondly, at that time at least the Minister of Finance was apprehensive of these favoured (nation treaties, and was unwilling to grant anything in the nature of a treaty or tariff arrangement which would entitle the favoured nations to favoured nation treatment in our market. Things have very greatly changed since then. At that time the favoured nations were not to participate; rather than that he would change the Bill, and the Bill was changed in the following year. But now, when this reciprocity of another kind is going through, the favoured nations are let in. I do not see how the minister or the government can reconcile the two positions. When dealing with England they would not allow the favoured nations in; but in dealing with the United States in the present pact, so anxious apparently are they to get .it through that they are willing to open the door so wide that thirteen other nations are allowed to participate without giving anything in return. That is one of the great objections to this agreement. With the United States it is very different. By their constitution their favoured nations do not participate with Canada in their market. When we are told that this looks like a fair arrangement to both countries, both giving up something and both getting something, that feature is entirely overlooked, and it has a very important effect.
Now, we are told that reciprocity when it existed in the old days brought prosperity. Well, certain interests in Canada were very prosperous. I have no desire to disparage reciprocity at that time or deal unfairly with it; but every man in this country knows that at that time, unfortunately for the powers engaged in it, but fortunately for us who had grain to sell, there was a very disastrous war in Europe, the Crimean war. For the first years of the reciprocity treaty wheat brought $2.50 a bushel in England. We participated in that prosperity. Whether we had reciprocity with the United States or not, tour wheat was (worth as much money as any other, or more, because of its superior quality, and we got no more for it by sending it to the States. Then during the latter part of that period, when the American war was raging, when teas of thousands of the farmers of the United. States had to abandon their husbandry operations and take the field, and when the price of foodstuffs and bread-stuffs soared high, we again participated in that prosperity. But it was not all prosperity in Canada at that time. Let me just refer to the shipping trade that languished during those years. Following the treaty, business in and out of the port of Montreal declined. The carrying trade of
