the St. Lawrence in 1854 was valued at $33,033,128. In the next year it dropped to $15,208,000. The ships' tonnage going to the sea from Montreal and Quebec decreased from 1,487,097 tons to 870,794, and the value of the exports from $42,000,000 to $28,000,000. On Canadian canals in the first fiscal year of the treaty the tolls fell off by 32 per cent. That in itself tells a very dismal tale of the effect of reciprocity, even at that early period, on the shipping and the foreign trade of the country.
We see that the shipping. declined in tonnage and in value. The canals did not do the same work, and there was not anything like the same volume of- business going through them. With the exception of the traffic going north and south there was very little business being transacted in the country compared with what there had been a year or two previous. But, our American friends were then after what they are now after. They were not so diligently in pursuit of it, it is true-still they were after it. I refer to the natural resources of this country. At that time the grass had not, so to speak, shortened for them. They still had a vast storehouse of natural resources, but as time has gone by this has been, pretty well drawn on. One of the main reasons, and one of the avowed reasons, is that the American people shall have access to our natural resources, and not only have access to them, but take them away to a foreign country and manufacture them with foreign labour.
Let me just point out what President Taft said about that:
Ought we not then to arrange a commercial agreement with Canada, if we can, by which we shall hare direct access to her great supply of natural products? Should we not now, therefore, before their policy has become too crystallized and fixed for change meet them in a spirit of real concession, facilitate commerce between the two countries, and thus greatly increase the natural resources available to our people? By giving our people access to the Canadian forests we shall reduce the consumption of our own which, in the hands of comparatively few owners now have a value that requires enlargement oLonr available timber resources.
This is explicitly one of the American main objects of reciprocity, and it is equally one of the main reasons why it should be opposed.
I would refer for a moment to an article which appeared in the London ' Times,' and which I think most fittingly puts the case to the Canadian people. Hon. gentlemen will, perhaps, recollect the correspondent of the 'Times' who headed his article during the last two or three months, ' The Buttering of Parsnips,' with special reference to the right hon. gentleman who leads this House (Sir Wilfrid Laurier).
Allow me to read an extract from one of these letters:
The short sighted man says, ' let us sell our wheat and our timber.' The long sighted man replies, ' no, let us sell our flour and biscuits and furniture and paper. Let us not sell our raw materials, hut the manufactured article. That is the only way in which we can reap the full profits on our products and establish ourselves in the community of interests that makes a nation.'
Surely no one could epitomize the protection of our natural resources in more clear language than this. ' But,' hon. gentlemen on the opposite side say, ' we are not going to interfere with your manufactured articles.' Well, the same writer in the same article deals with that under the caption ' The Spider and the Fly.' He say®:
You say it is restricted reciprocity, and we will go no further. But you remember the fable: the spider invited the fly to step into his parlour. The fly replied, ' I will only put in one foot, the rest of me will remain outside.' The spider was satisfied. Why? Because he knew the foot would stick.
What does that show? It shows that when the farmer finds his goods give him very little if any advance in price, and that all he produces is open to competition, and that he has no protection in anything he raises, but has to pay duty on everything he buys, he will not be satisfied. If the farmer realizes that he has to suffer competition from American farm products, I think there will be a very great hue and cry throughout the country.
The timber question was mentioned by President Taft, as it has been mentioned by many others. Two authorities on the subject who ought to be acceptable to the Liberal people of this country, are Senator Ross and the Hon. Mr. Sifton.. These are two gentlemen who have gone on record as being directly opposed to this treaty, especially so far as timber is concerned.
I do not desire to take up the time of the House with the reading of Senator Ross's remarks, suffice it to say that he has gone flatfooted on record as being in opposition to the treaty with special regard to lumber, and in that respect he quotes, with approval, what was said by the Hon. Clifford Sifton, as chairman of the Commission on Natural Resources-or as we call it now, the Conservation Commission. It is well to read and heed the warning of Mr. Sifton, who says:
At the end of 20 years the United States would have no timber for sale, in the ordinary way. In Canada the supply was large, but if the supply in the United States ran out, the supply in Canada would last the United States for only seven years. The time must come, however, when the people of Canada would demand legislation prohibiting the export of marketable timber.

That is the natural view, and the only view which will do justice to Canadian interests.	,
Now, not only is this government, by its treaty, not protecting and conserving our resources, and especially our timber resources-not only is it not heeding the warning of the chairman of its own commission-a commission constituted for the purpose of collecting information, but it is exposing these very resources to the free exploitation of the American trust man and combine man, because by taking down the duty on timber or by making it free, you will no doubt give the lumberman of this country a very large and immediate profit on his timber, but we must bear in mind that much of this timber which is growing on this Canadian soil of ours is owned by Americans. We have no desire to interfere with any man's property rights in this country, but there is no reason why the exploiter should be facilitated in denuding and depleting our country of its natural resources, and of its timber in particular.
Both liberals and conservatives talk with pride and with pleasure about our great country. We are in the habit of hearing Canada praised, and it pleases us. Our British brethren, as well as foreigners all join in one accord in complimenting this country upon its almost inexhaustible store of natural resources. How, I ask in the name of common sense, are we to preserve these resources if they are not protected from exploitation? If any one and every one can come in and take out timber, our minerals, &c., at a nominal figure, as they have in the past, what benefit is it to Canada? Many of these resources might just as well be in Egypt or in Russia if thev are simply for the exploiter, to be removed in the rough or natural state.
What benefit is it to the country? Take an American lumberman who came here years ago, and bought blocks of virgin forest for a trifle-what benefit is it to this country if he is allowed to take out that timber in the rough. Of what benefit are any of our natural resources unless there is some guardianship, some protection, some conservation? For these resources are inter-dependent. If you remove the timber, you make less favourable the conditions of agriculture. And so in other matters. But of what avail is it for us to boast of our great natural resources if those resources are to be exploited by any one who chooses to come and acquire them? The only affect is to make the rich man richer, and the poor poorer. The lumberman who has acquired the timber will increase his revenues-to him that hath shall be given. But what will become of the mechanic or farmer who wishes to buy lumber? Why, the great consuming public will have to pay , Mr. MACDONELL.
more for their lumber than in the past. And that is one of the features of this pact that is most frequently attacked. It is said, and said truly in my opinion, that it is a pact for the trusts and combines; it will leave this country exposed, as the United States has been exposed to the exploitation of these men. A moment's reflection will cause one to realize that the American trusts and combines will extend their operations to this country. They are anxious to do it; they seek to enlarge their area from which to draw the resources they need. That is why this pact is welcomed so cordially in the United States.
Now, it does seem to me that the home market for the producer of this country is the best market. It is said that the home market is not large enough, but we know that about 80 or 85 per cent of all that is produced in this country is used in this *oountiry. We know that the home market has built up our neighbours to the south, and that the farmer in that country has been the best advocate of the factory. And so he should be, because the factory assures him of customers for what he raises. Let me quote on this subject no less an authority than Mr. Wilson, Secretary of Agriculture for the United States. He fills the position occupied by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fisher), who is now leading the House, and I think that hon. gentlemen will agree that the Minister of Agriculture should, and in some cases does, know a great deal about the agricultural conditions of his country. Mr. Wilson said:
The American farmer brought about the building of the American factory, because he wanted a home market. That home market is the best to be found anywhere, because our people all live well and are all able to buy the best farm produce,-that is, all who are willing to work. It may be said, without much exaggeration, that the American farmer is responsible for the upbuilding of the factory. He has voted steadily for half a century to give protection to the extent of the difference in cost of production between this country and any country that desires to sell in our markets. Was that right or wrong? Was it wise for the farmers to do that? There was no market at home. They wanted a market as near the factory as they could bring it. Now millions of people who work in these factories and in occupations other than farming want food at reasonable prices. Who can condemn them for that desire?
All that is said by Mr. Wilson can be truly said by the Minister of Agriculture of this country. We are now embarking, as it were, upon the period that they have passed, we are experiencing the same conditions here that they experienced in their country a very few years ago, and we are finding that the best market for the farmers' produce, is in the towns and cities which are built un around the factories. Therefore, it

seems to me that the true policy of the government is not to alarm the commercial and manufacturing industries as they have done, but by every reasonable means consistent with the keeping of prices at fair levels, they should encourage the home market, affording protection which, as Mr. Wilson says, is enough to place the home producer, having regard to the higher labour cost of his product, on an equality with the producer abroad. If that policy were adhered to, our market would be found in our own country, we should have a large influx of the farming community, and much greater stability of our manufacturing and business interests.
Hon. gentlemen opposite, especially the Minister of Finance, have spoken of members of the Conservative party having made many journeys to Washington. Well, they were not the only ones who did that. Members of the Liberal party, on many occasions, when in opposition, and since they were returned to power, have made these same trips. One gentleman went on many occasions-the late John Charlton. He attended the National Reciprocity Convention at Washington, on November 19, and 20, 1901. He was there pleading for reciprocity, and holding out inducements for them to enter into an arrangement with us. I do not believe hon. gentlemen opposite will repudiate Mr. Charlton. Here is the picture he painted for the Americans of what reciprocity would do for them. He gave quite a lengthy address. He said in part:
What we want is reciprocal free trade in natural products, as I remarked a moment ago, we buy three times as much in the way of agricultural products as we sell to the United States. With free trade the whole vast mining region of British Columbia and the Yukon districts would draw its supplies of food from Oregon and Washington. The maritime provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island would draw nineteen-twentieths of their food supplies from the seaboard cities of the United States, and vessels bringing coal and lumber from those provinces would take back cargoes of flour, meal, &c., as return cargoes. The mining and lumbering regions of Ontario and Quebec would buy enormously of American farm products.
Now that would be very interesting reading foT the farmers of British Columbia, the maritime provinces, of Ontario and Quebec. AH these provinces were to be supplied with their foodstuffs by the American farmers. That is the exact condition today. Mr. Charlton was then speaking about a reciprocal tariff in natural products, just what we are asked to adopt to-day, and this is the inducement he offered the American people. We did not hear anything of that . kind in this country. There, he was speaking his convictions, he was away from 314
home, he was addressing strangers, and no doubt felt at liberty to unbutton himself and tell the people what was in his heart. And that was in his heart, that all the food supplies of these provinces should be drawn from the American people. Now the farmer here is told, as a reason why he should endorse this pact; it is going to improve everything; you are going to have the Augustan age in the rural districts of Canada, you are going to have a golden period; all you raise is going to bring very high prices; farms are going to improve in value, everything you have is going to be made more valuable; you are going to enter into a golden heritage, and practically your working days are over. Now let us see what effect this market of 90 millions of people has had upon the farming community in the States, and then we can form some opinion as to how reciprocity will affect farm values in Canada. It certainly will not improve them, if statistics are to be believed. Here is the record:
Advocates of reciprocity are making statements to the effect that the adoption of reciprocity will immediately increase the value of Canadian farm lands 25 per cent or more. Instead of making wild guesses let us get at the facts. Since the reciprocity negotiations began the United States government has had a report prepared by experts showing the comparative value per acre of improved farm lands in 1900 and 1910 in various border states and in the Canadian provinces adjoining them. This report states that between 1990 and 1910 the value of improved farm lands increased 67 per cent in Maine, 37 per cent in New Hampshire, 33 per cent in Vermont, 181 per cent in Nova Scotia, 120-per cent in New Brunswick, 70 per cent in Prince Edward Island, 80 per cent in Quebec, 43 per cent in Ontario, 39 per cent in Michigan, 77 per cent in Minnesota, 123 per cent in Manitoba, 201 per cent in Saskatchewan and 185 per cent in Alberta.
Now with this great market at the dooTS of the American farmers, we find nevertheless that their farms have not increased in value at anything like the same ratio as have the farms of the Canadian provinces adjoining. They have a market of ninety millions of people, where i;s their increased value? This big market does not seem to have brought riches to them. It may be said that the great increase in the value of our western lands is unusual because it is a new country. That may be so. But why the increase in the value of the farms of the older provinces? Look at the enormous increase in the value of farm land in the province of the Minister of Finance himself, most phenomenal, 181 per cent increase in Nova Scotia. Surely nothing better than that could be desired. It is two or three times the ratio of increase in the American States adjoining, and yet the farmers of this country are asked to make this change. Let us see what will happen

if the tariff wall is taken down and natural products are allowed to pass freely between the two countries. Of course, the tendency and effect will be to produce a uniformity in *values. Land is only worth what it will produce. If all the territory is practically cne great field of agriculture, you are going to have the value of the farm lands on both sides brought down to something like uniformity. You will not have this great increase in value continuing in our Canadian farms, because the value will necessarily be brought down to the level of American farms, the same as the value of the produce on those farms. Granting that the quality of the land is the same, it seems to me that is self-evident.
Now permit me to make an allusion to the opinions of some prominent public men in the United States with regard to what is likely to happen when this treaty goes into effect. Senator Albert B. Cummins, of Iowa, is a well known public man who has delivered a great many speeches on this subject, in the Senate and elsewhere in the United States. In a very able article in the 'Editorial Keview' he says many things which are well worthy of reproduction. I will extract the following:
With respect to live stock. I have taken some pains to discover what relative prices are, comparing Canada and the United States, and this is the result: the average value of horses in the United States is $108.10; in Canada, $133. Dairy cows in the United States, $35.79; in Canada, $43. Other cattle, without respect to age or grade, in the United States, $19.41; in Canada, $31. Sheep in the United States, $4.08; in Canada, $6. Hogs in the United States, $9.14; in Canada, $11.
Bearing in mind what has been already said, I predict that with nearly everything, except wheat, barley, and possibly hay, our exports of agricultural products into Canada will grow more rapidly than the imports of such products into the United States from Canada.
That is a very important statement, and if it is true, as we are told, that the American people now sell to us $3 worth for every dollar's worth we sell to them, what is likely to take place after this treaty goes into effect?
If, as Senator Cummins says, we are going to import into Canada very much more than they are going to import of our products, what is the ratio going to be?-six to one probably, or it may be double. So that instead of trade getting better between ourselves and the United States in so far as we are concerned it will get worse because, with the exception of two items, and possibly a third, in that long list, Senator Cummins is of opinion that the Americans will sell much more largely to us than we will sell to them. He ought to know. He is a well informed public man, he understands their capacity to export, he knows the surplus of the country, Mr. MACDONELL.
he knows what the prices are there and here and he makes that very deliberate statement advisedly.
I would like to make one more reference to Mr. Wilson. Mr. Wilson is the American Secretary of Agriculture, and he refers incidentally to a matter which has been very much discussed in this country. He refers to the milling industry. In an article in the 'Editorial Review' of May, he says:
I am firmly convinced that it would be to the advantage of both countries for us to take the export wheat of Canada, mill it and send the flour to the markets of the world, because the dairymen of the United States would then get the by-products of the mills and as the population of the United States increases, the dairy market will be greater and greater. Wo will get those by-products then, instead of having the wheat go as wheat to foreign countries where the by-products would be sold and used to great advantage by dairymen in those countries.	*
Mr. Wilson ought to know pretty well the capabilities of his country in that respect. He says candidly what many people in this country have said and have been called alarmists for saying, namely, that the wheat of this country, especially the No. 1 hard grade of wheat, would be exported to the United States and there milled. It is quite obvious, it is self-evident what the advantages will _ be to the American people from the milling of the wheat in their country. As Mr. Wilson very candidly puts it, their dairymen will have the benefit of the by-products. He, however, facetiously says that this will be good for both countries because the wheat of Canada will go to their country for milling purposes. How the benefit will come to Canada from milling Canadian wheat in Minneapolis and other wheat milling centres is more than I can tell. But, he is not concerned with Canada. He supposes that the interests of this country are being looked after by the public men of this country. He is a public man in the American union, and he is looking after the interests of that country, and apparently doing it very well. He points out very naturally, very properly, what an advantage it will be if the milling of our wheat is carried on in that country. We all know that although a comparatively large amount of wheat is produced in this country at the present time, still we are not by any means the first, or second, or third, or fourth wheat producing country in the world. The United States produces a very vast amount of wheat, more than any other country; Russia, I think comes next; France is a very large wheat producing country, then there is the Argentine Republic and possibly one other country. I think that all of these countries, at least produce a greater quantity of wheat than

we do. But, in proportion to the quantity of wheat grown in these different countries no country exports the same percentage of the quantity grown as Canada does. Although our wheat production is praiseworthy, although it is encouraging, there is such a large home consumption of wheat in these other countries that the percentage of wheat produced in the country and exported from Canada is larger, I think than the percentage grown and exported by any other country.	The export of our wheat becomes a very important matter. We are going to export an increasingly large quantity of wheat. Just in proportion to the quantity of wheat we export will rise and increase the importance of where that wheat will be milled. It is altogether unnecessary for any man to argue that it is a good thing for a country to mill its own wheat because not only does it give the millers employment, and all the incidental benefits and profits that arise from a great industry of that kind, but in addition to this, and perhaps of still greater importance is the fact that where the milling takes place the by-products remain. That is a most important thing. The by-products cannot be profitably shipped to any great distance, and it is all important that the wheat should be milled in this country, that the industry should remain in this country, and that the by-products and the benefits derived from these by-products should remain here.
I think it is only fair to say that perhaps the east and west feature of this agreement has been argued at very great length. But, if we are going to have this treaty, every man knows-it is self-evident-that to a very great extent the east and west transportation of this country is going to decrease. How much no one can tell. We know it from the history of the reciprocity treaty of 1854 that in the very next year after the treaty went into force there was an instantaneous and immense falling off in the shipment through the canals going east, and west, and from the ports of Montreal and Quebec. Their shipping declined one-half practically in one year. With that example before us, and with our certain knowledge that history repeats itself when identical conditions are re-created we do know that there will be a great decline in the east and west transportation shipping of this country. How much no one can tell. We have not heard so much of the all-red route since this pact has been before the people. That seems to have dropped and very naturally and very properly so because I do not know just what it will have to do. Where will it take the traffic? What occasion will there be for it? We are getting along pretty well at the present time with our present conditions. The all red-route was 314J
proclaimed in anticipation of a largely increased shipping business to and from the ocean ports of this country. It is quite evident that that is not going to happen. There is a very significant and a very important silence upon that question.
Now, with regard to the east and west route, it is rather wonderful that the past statements of the government seem to be entirely forgotten by members of the government themselves and largely by the public. Therefore it is necessary perhaps to refer occasionally to what was said by the leaders of this government in regard to the east and west traffic of the country, especially in regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. I would like to refer to some statements made by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). When speaking on the Grand Trunk Pacific and National Transcontinental railway in the House of Commons we recollect perhaps this rather striking statement:
Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:
Heaven grant that if be not already too late; heaven grant that whilst we tarry and dispute, the trade of Canada is not deviated to other channels, and that an ever vigilant competitor does not take to himself the trade that properly belongs to those who acknowledge Canada as their native or their adopted land.
And the right hon. gentleman was followed by his Minister of Finance on the same occasion who said:
It is desirable that we should give our American brethren to understand that Canada is resolved to work out her independence in these things, and the present proposal will promote this object, and that even if still another railway should be necessary we shall be prepared to construct it. The attitude that the government has taken upon the subject . . . has already attracted much attention across the border, and there is much keener appreciation of Canada's independence than ever before.
The Minister of Finance was out herod- [DOT] ing his chief; he was prepared to build two Transcontinental railways to move the trade of Canada east and west so that we might be for all time independent of our American friends. The very bargain itself with the Grand Trunk Pacific contains penal clauses compelling the railway to carry the trade east and west to Canadian ports. Section 43 of the contract which now forms part of the bill reads:
43. The company further agrees that it shall not, in any matter within its power, directly or indirectly advise or encourage the transportation of such freight by routes other than those above provided, but shall, in all respects, in good faith, use its utmost endeavours to fulfil the conditions upon which public aid is granted, namely,-the development of trade through Canadian channels and Canadian ocean ports.

Do I need to remind toon, gentlemen that the very same principle was embodied in the British North America Act with regard to the Intercolonial railway, declaring that it was essential to the consolidation of the union of British North America, and this same principle of east and west transportation was incorporated in the agreement with British Columbia in 1871, it being made an essential part of the union that the Canadian Pacific railway should be built. This is proof that in all sections of this country and at all times in her history there has been uppermost in the minds of the people of Canada the necessity for this east and west route until now this government agreed with the United States that her trade shall be diverted to the south. American public men are gloating over the fact that the American ocean ports are to handle our export freight, and I commend to the government the views of Governor Foss, of Massachussetts, who is strongly for the agreement, because he believes it will draw all kinds of trade away from Canadian ports; that there will he no more Montreal, or St. John, or Halifax, but that Boston is to be the great port for shipment of Canadian goods. We know only too well that that is most likely what will happen if this pact goes through. It seems most extraordinary that the right hon. gentleman and his Minister of Finance should have turned around in their own tracks, and gone back on their declared policy and are now proposing by this pact to undo much of what has been done by the legislation of past years to encourage national transcontinental east and west routes. Why, the right hon gentleman, who declared so often against reciprocity should now favour it, we do not know, but there may be a rteason that will come to the surface later on. In the House of Commons at banquets and on other public occasions, and at the Colonial Conference we find him of late years pronouncing against reciprocity. In 1891 he fell fighting for reciprocity or commercial union or continental free trade or whatever you may choose to call it, and from that date to the date of this agreement he seems to have been opposed to it. In 1899 he said:
If we know the hearts and minds of our people at present, I think I am not making too wide a statement when I say that the general feeling in Canada is not in favour of reciprocity. There was a time when Canadians would have given many things to obtain the American market. There was a time when the market of the great cities of the Union was the only market we had, hut these days are past and over now. We are not dependent on the American market now.
At a banquet in Montreal in 1901 the right hon. gentleman declared:

do without British capital? What would the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) do with regard to financing his loans? Perhaps the credit of Canada is now good enough to go to the European markets, but where does it naturally go? To the London money market of course. There is not a city or town in Canada whose streets are not lighted or paved or whose public utilities are not operated more or less by British capital, which was got at a time when capital could not be got at the same rate of interest from foreign countries. This capital is invested in exploiting the mines -it is invested in our agricultural lands- it is invested in every walk and sphere of our national life, and there is nothing more closely associated with business in Canada. It has always been so, and will continue so if we maintain our trade conditions as they are at the present time. How long these conditions will last if we are going to pass over our gold and silveT to pay for American products, is a thing I do not know.
There is another matter kindred with the one of which I am now speaking. The right hon. gentleman has been full of hope that some day we would obtain a British preference. We on this side of the House have indulged the same hope and desire. What can bk more advantageous to the great farming community of this country than some preference on the British markets for food stuffs they need and which we raise? Now, this is a hope which has some prospect of ultimately materialising. In fact some of the British public men are now committed to it-and when I say this I do not mean some of the men of to-day or yesterday, because the matter has been before them for the last ten or fifteen years, and they have been advocating the adoption of some preference for the products of the overseas portions of the empire. I have every reason to expect that when the time is ripe and proper some form of preference will be obtained by the overseas portions of the empire in the home market of Great Britain.
The agreement ignores one objection which has been urged with force and persistence in Canada. It has been contended that with free trade in natural products between Canada and the United States, reciprocal treatment of Canadian products in British markets would become impossible, inasmuch as American products would seek an outlet at Canadian ports in order to secure the benefit of British preferential duties. Certainly Canada has faced no such radical change in fiscal policy since the system of protection was established over thirty years ago.
Now, how can we hope to succeed in getting that preference if the proposed treaty passes? How can we expect a British pref-Mr. MACDONELL.
erence if all the food stuffs and natural products of the American nation are at liberty to swarm over the border line into this country, and be reshipped to Great Britain as the products of this country? Surely: that would make a British preference impossible, and it seems to me natural that it should be so, because the preference would be given to us as part of the overseas dominions of the British Empire. It would not be given to the products of the United States. Now, if reciprocity is enforced between ourselves and our American neighbours, it is, of course, quite obvious that their products would come in here, and intermingle with ours in such a way that there would be no possibility of distinguishing between the two, the result would be that Great Britain would naturally say: ' It is impossible for us to admit your products into our markets when they are accompanied by a great avalanche of American products which we cannot distinguish from your own.
The hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) when introducing this measure, spoke delightfully about the certainty and the uncertainty of the duration of the pact. He told us in one sentence that this would only be a temporary affair-that if we did not like it we were not bound to anybody for any .time-and if it were found to be inconvenient or unprofitable we could undo it, and revert to our former condition-that we did not have to abide by it, but could cancel it at any time. In the next, sentence he told us that the hope was expressed 'by both prties to the transaction that it would be found profitable and that it would be enduring.
Let us see what the opinion of our American friends is as to the enduring of it. Mr. McCall, who introduced the measure into the House said in the debate on the reciprocity agreement:
It is scarcely good form for us to regulate in advance, the internal fiscal policy of the British Empire. It will, however, always be within the power of Congress, if it shall appear that any undue advantage is hereafter given to Great Britain, to correct and change these rates, or repeal them all.
Before the pact goes into force, Mr. McCall says: ' If this does not suit us we are going to repeal it.' There is a condition of uncertainty created which is in itself, a very grave objection. We all know that the commercial interests of any country strive and struggle for one thing more than all others, and that is certainty and stability. Certainty of tariff and stability of trade. They cannot get on with a tariff which is changeable like -amoving .picture show, and which may alter at any moment-new scenes being rung up, and brought into the arena. That is not a condition which the

mercantile and manufacturing classes in this country desire. It is quite obvious that that kind of a temporary tariff would be most injurious. It would not be a stable condition of affairs, after diverting our routes of transportation north and south, after changing our trade conditions, and adopting our commercial life to the new conditions, to have all this suddenly overthrown and wiped out. What condition would trade be in then? ' Disorganization ' is scarcely a fair word to express the condition in which we would find ourselves.
The hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) took exception to a remark which I made regarding his statement in Montreal.
I have it before me now. Speaking at the Windsor Hall, Montreal, on March 25, 1911, the hon. minister said:
We know that a great many things have been said about this agreement which are wrong; we know that a great many men have formed their opinions in relation to this measure without adequate information, and so it is our desire that as opportunities occur, we shall endeavour to remove some of the misunderstandings which exist.
If the people have not had adequate information regarding this agreement who is to blame? Surely, the government. It may be, with the extraordinary and undue haste that has characterized the government's action, they could not prepare for our people proper information on this subject. But apparently our American friends were warned 'and advised in advance. They had their information all prepared, and much of what has been used in this House and throughout this country is information we have gleaned from American sources. Had full information been before the country when this pact was brought into the House, there would not have been the lengthy discussion upon it. We on this side have insisted that the people should have the information necessary to form an opinion upon this question. Every man in this country is as much entitled to information upon the nature of this pact as were the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and the Minister of Customs (Mr. Fater-son) when they were discussing it. It is an essential and fundamental change in our economic and national conditions. Every man. is affected by it, and every man is entitled to the means of forming an opinion upon the matter.
The opposition have condemned and opposed this pact in the belief that it is bad for Canada and for British interests. That, of course, is merely an opinion. But what we have tried to insist upon was that the people should have the information necessary to form an opinion in the first place, and in the second place that they should be afforded an opportunity to express that opinion. We believe that the people may
be trusted. And we believe that on this subject the people are being educated. Notwithstanding the complete absence of information brought down by the government, the people are getting the information. Public men are arising everywhere to spread the knowledge of the subject and people who are not in public life at all are engaged taking part in the work of public education. We hope the people will be given an opportunity of expressing themselves, pro and con on this question. That is all that the opposition asks. We believe that the people may be trusted; but we believe also that when the people's voice is heard on this subject it will be, not unanimously, of course, but by a^ heavy preponderance in opposition to this pact.

Mr. Chairman, I assure you of my sympathy in having to sit up so .late listening to this debate. Perhaps you are tired because of hearing only from one side. And we on this side also are not only somewhat tired, but almost ashamed that in the House of Commons, representing this great Canada, we have a majority who sit as dumb as oysters. We know that these gentlemen have ability to discuss this question if they wish to do so. We also understand that they are taking advantage of their position for the purpose, as they think, of letting this side talk itself out. I do not know that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) who is now leading tne House is going to accomplish exactly what he has set out to do. But I am sure that every member on this side-I would like to include the ' colony,' but I am perfectly satisfied I speak for all the Conservatives -is willing to remain here until this time next year if our humble efforts may protect the interest of the people. Surely, we could have no other desire at heart than the interest of the people to leave our homes and businesses and come here to remain during the sweltering July nights, impairing our health, to carry on the debate on this question.
I feel it my duty to address this House, becaue my constituents have sent me here not to sit dumb, but to express to the powers that be my views on the questions before the House. It is not for me to say how hon. gentlemen on the other side shall meet their constituents and explain why they did not take part in the debate. Only a few of them have taken part. But apparently they would rather leave unsaid what they believe to be the right thing for the people, than to say what they would have to say under the dictation of the gentleman who leads the House. We on this side, thank God, are left untrammelled; no lash is applied to us. Who can think

of our leader doing as the leaders of gentlemen opposite did?-going down to Washington where no doubt, the president entertained him kindly and gave him a good time. He certainly made them feel good and they evidently thought it their duty to tie this'-(in their eyes)-little Canada to the United States. We on this side take issue with them. I have lived on the borders of the United States for many years and have had dealings with people of the United States. In the many dealings I have had with them, I always took the precaution-perhaps it is because I am Scotch-to have my wits about me before I attempted1 to trade with them. It would have been well for this * country if these gentlemen, before they hied down to Washington, had taken the precaution to be well on their guard. But, instead of that, they did not give any hint to the people of this country of what they were going to do at Washington. If they knew, they knew it when they went the previous year to do a little dickering with these same gentlemeji in Washington. It is my belief that the' gentlemen who went last fall to Washington to make this pact had promised the American negotiators that next year they would give them a little more. Now we find these two gentlemen tying up the people of this country to a pact which, I am satisfied, the majority of the Canadian people do not want, and won't stand for. The Conservative party in this House are numerically not as strong as the government party, but I think we represent, perhaps, the maiority of the people of Canada. We conscientiously feel it is our duty to oppose this pact in the interests, as we think, of the great majority of the people of Canada. We believe that it has been entered into without due consideration. We believe that there are no two men sitting in this House who are able to go to Washington and, off their own bat, to use a slang phrase, negotiate intelligently concerning every interest. that they are going either to make or to break.
Now. Sir, I understand that the hon. the Minister of Finance is neither a lumberman, a miller, a merchant, or a manufac-turere. I think he is a retired gentleman,
Mr. SMYTH (ATgoirnL
or soon will be. We know that the other negotiator, the hon. the Minister of Customs, makes very nice candies, very nice cakes, and all that sort of thing; he makes crackers, but he has given us a cracker now that we don't want to take. I have had some experience in life myself. I have not been a baker, but I have been a blacksmith, a soldier, a sailor and a farmer, and I would hate to take upon my shoulders to s?y that I knew all about either farming, or soldiering, or anything else in connection with the industrial life of this country. I contend that the two gentlemen who went to Washington knew but very little gbout the lumber interests of this country. If they had been alive to the lumber interests they would not have allowed the Americans to draw the wool over their eyes as they have done. It is of course well known that lumber has been allowed to come into this- country free for years; we have -had free lumber entering Canada from the United States for several years. We had been up against a $2 per thousand duty, until a short time ago, upon our lumber going into the United States. Now, as I understand this pact, lumber is going into the United States free. That looks all very well on the face of it. But how does our lumber compare with the lumber that is coming into Canada free of duty? It is well known that lumber is not manufactured) solely into boards. Lumber has to be manufactured into other articles; it has to be planed, tongued and grooved in many instances, thereby not only reducing its weight because of the dressing, but reducing its weight because of the fact that it has to be dried before it is dressed. Now, the United States very carefully shut out dressed or partly dressed lumber. They knew that if we had to ship all rough lumber into the United States from the interior of Canada, lumber in its rough state, the addition to the weight of that lumber, in comparison with what it would be if it was dried and planed, would more than offset the price of lumber in its dressed state. When we talk of lumber we do not mean simply boards. Now, the Americans very wisely objected to allowing our shingles to go free into the United States. It is a well-known ' fact that the lumbermen to-day, in order to make a living and a fair profit out of their industry have to utilize every bit of the timber that is standing on their limits.
It is a well-known fact that to-day the lumbermen are using up material, odds and ends, for lath, &c., that they wouldn't look at fifteen or twenty years ago. But

speechtext: The protection remains the same in Canada; it is not touched one iota.

I quite understand that it is not touched one iota, but you did not take advantage of the fact of being there. When you had the opportunity you could have placed $2 a thousand feet on lumber coming into this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But we did not want to do that.
Why? If you had been wide-awake and understood your business you would have done something for the lumber interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We think it is bad policy; we do not want it.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman is not aware of the fact that the Americans require the better grades of our white pine lumber. They do not require our lower grades stuff such as hemlock and spruce (other than pulp wood), and lo_w grade pine. There are lumbermen within the sound of my voice now who will tell you that every mill yard in northern Ontario at least is piled high with the lower grades of lumber that southern pine comes in competition with in this country. The profit perhaps of their whole operations is in the cull end of the lumber and how they can best market it. If they have a failure in marketing the cull end of their lumber they usually make no profits that year at least. Our Canadian lumbermen in _ my district-I do not refer to the American
lumbermen-claim that instead of getting lumber into the United States free they would rather have had an import duty on southern pine coming into this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is that the Conservative policy?

I am talking from the standpoint of the lumbermen's interests. I am trying to show the hon. gentleman that he did not know his business when he went to Washington, and I think I have succeeded perhaps in convincing him, because at least I got a response from him, that it would be to the interest of the lumber industry to shut out the southern pine as against our low grade lumber. I think that the hon. gentleman will agree with me in that respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I do not. I say it is not in the interest of Canada to increase the lumber duties at all, and if it is the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite to increase the lumber duties let them say so.
They are Grit organizers now.

Every man of them is a Grit organizer under the guise of a grain grower. But after the campaign of education that was carried on a few weeks ago by a very able member of this House, there are not so many of them sticking so closely to the so-called leaders of the grain growers. I had the honour and pleasure of b|eing in the west myself for a few weeks, and I met a great many of the grain growers. I met a good many of the gentlemen who came down here demanding that the government should assist them in several ways, and wient back convinced that the government were going to do something for them in connection with this reciprocity pact or something else. But when thiey found out that they were humbugged and sold out, that their so-called leaders were nothing but political heelers who had been trading on their credulity and tb(eir name as grain growers, they abandoned them, and to-day we do not find all the gentlemen who were here backing up those who stayed over the day after to confer with the premier staying with the machine. Now, the grain growers of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta are a very intelligent class of men, especially those I met, and they had only to be shown that they were being misled by the so-called leaders of the Grain Growers' Association to realize the position that they had placed themselves in. In travelling through the west, I found one or two of my friends who were inclined to be in favour of reciprocity, one friend especially, a very intelligent sort of chap; but he had been hob-nobbing with bad company politically; and when I asked him to tell me just how
he understood this reciprocity pact, he said, in the first place, the government is going to allow implements to come free into this country.' I said, 'Who told you that?' He said, 'the leaders of the Grain Growers' Association; and they issued pamphlets in my own riding telling the farmers that they were going to have free implements. If that is the kind of campaign with which this government think they are going to carry the country next time, they are gpeatly mistaken, because the farmers today are too wideawake to be humbugged with any such nonsense as that. While some who do not read very much may be persuaded at the first blush that that is the case, by discussion with their neighbours they soon become enlightened. That is the process going on through the west, and it leads the government to question whether they should give the west redistribution and increasjed representation. We on this side of the House want to see the west properly represented; we shall be glad to see its representation trebled. The west deserves it, because to my mind it is the greatest part of this country agriculturally, and in many other respects. Our friends opposite wepe very cocky a few months ago about what they were going to do when they got increased representation from the west. They arie not so anxious now; they want to put off the evil day as far as they can. Now, we do not fear going to the country on this reciprocity pact. We will welcome the election at the earliest moment, and you can throw in a few bush polls if you think they will strengthen your chances very much, because your Waterloo on this verj question is not very far distant, if I read the minds of the people of Canada aright. We are accused now of having all the wealth behind us, of being imperial jingoes, and last night I was sorry to se-e the Minister of Finance lose his temper and accuse us of being obstructionists and of reading from newspapers. I would like to know where we arie going to get our information if we do not read from newspapers, because we cannot get it from the government. I often wondier whether they are to compile it or not; they certainly have not produced it here, and I do not think they want to produce it. I will not bother the House by reading much from newspapers, but 1 have a few documents here that I would like to read from, and they will be very interesting. It may take two or three hours to read one of them alone; but there has been so much reference to former treaties that I think it would be well to have thesernat-ters placed on Hansard so that they will be in the hands of every member of this House and of every citizen of Canada, and I am sure that the hon. gentleman who is leading the House to-night will bear with me an hour or two while I read part of that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Certainly, with great pleasure.

Before I take up that document, I want to take up another matter in connection with this pact. We are told that there is no danger of annexation-that the United States can get all 'the advantages of us they like, they can own us root and branch, but we will still be British subjects. That is a grand feeling to have, that we will be able to control ourselves in that way, even when the United 'Stateis controls everything ,we have. I would rather remain, feeling that the mother country was going to have a firm and solid hold on Canada for all time to come, than see the United States get one dollar's worth of our products, because we can live splendidly without them. Many years ago they told us repeatedly that annexation or starvation was staring us in the face. They told us and the outside world that we were hardly civilized, that we would never be able to take care of ourselves or build railways, because we had no land to build on except a little strip along the front.
They found, Sir, they were mistaken in that. They found that we had the land, that we had the men, and that we had the money, they also found that we did not have to go to the United States to get the money, but we went to the dear old land to get it to build our railways and our canals and our public works throughout Canada.
They have realized that while Canada may be small in their eyes, still she is great in the financial world, able to stand alone, and do splendidly without their assistance, they also realized that the natural products of this country are" far in excess of the resources of their country and colonies put together, and they realize that in the paper industry, and many other industries they are absolutely dependent on Canada for the material to carry on their business. They are also dependent on Canada for their nickel. It is a well known fact that near the district I represent we have the greatest nickel mines in the world. It is also a well known fact that every one of these mines is owned by Americans. No doubt these gentlemen would be very glad to see us annexed to the United States.
As I said, Canada is greater in the eyes of the United States to-day than they ever dreamt she would be. They see our natural resources, our nickel, our timber, our wheat and everything else, and they are most anxious now to trade with us. I think if the hon. gentlemen who went down there had one ounce of pluck in their breasts, when they were invited to go they would have said: Nay. We want none of you. You turned us back many a time.

Now we will turn you back.' Instead of that they hobnobbed with these American gentlemen and had the wool pulled over their eyes. The result is that to-day they want to bind Canada hard and fast to the United States, which will be nothing more or less than the forerunner of annexation. In this reciprocity agreement I see the danger of the United States having control of our markets, and of our industries, and I see that their eye single is to-day on Canada. They have turned our ministers back in years gone by and when they did so the Liberal party was very jubilant in its criticism of the manner in which the gentlemen from Canada went over to the United States. Would it not be just nice, when Canada is big in the eyes of the United States, and when she is in a position to give them some of their own medicine, that they should get it just when they asked our ministers to go over there? There was some excuse for our ministers in years gone by asking to have a little trade with their big brother, the United States, but there was no excuse for this government interfering with the w'heels of commerce, or interfering with every financial interest throughout the length and breadth of this country by hanging over our heads a pact which is disagreeable, offensive, and I think, unconstitutional.
We, on this side of the House, ask you, Sir, to give us an opportunity to show that the people of Canada endorse the doctrine we have been preaching along that line. There cannot be anything fairer or more reasonable than that we should go to the people who elected us on that question. I do not think we are in any less position as regards a mandate than the right hon. gentleman and the hon. gentlemen who sit on the treasury benches, leading this government. The votes of the people were not given at the last election or the election previous on a question such as this at all. It was not before them, and they did not know anything about it.
I think we must give some weight to the sayings of the gentlemen who occupy the positions of senators and representatives in the United States. What do we find? We find these gentlemen saying that one of the advantages to be derived by the United States if this pact went through, would be that it would lead to greater things, along the line of annexation. We have been told that these gentlemen were not serious. Well, we might just as well say that the hon. gentleman who introduced this pact to the House was not serious.
President Taft knew something about our forests. He took the pains to educate himself and find out all about them, and a great deal about our other industries as well. While this government does not

know anything about our forests, the Americans can give us all the information we want about them. They know more about our natural resources than we ever dreamt of knowing.
As you know President Taft is a very large man in the United States-nearly as big a man in his country as the right hon. the leader of the House is here. Surely, we must give him credit for being serious in what he said-surely President Taft is not trying to jolly somebody all the time, as he did our ministers. He said:
Should we not then arrange a commercial agreement with Canada, if we can, by which we will have direct access to her great supply of natural products?
And here is something further. Shortly afterwards the president spoke at Columbus, Ohio, and said:
The greatest reason for adopting this agreement is the fact that it i5 going to unite two countries with kindred people, and lying together across a wide continent in a commercial and social union.
Next Mr. Taft went to Atlanta, and while there he developed his idea of commercial union. This is what he said:
When we entered upon the negotiations X asked the Secretary of State and his commissioners to offer free trade in everything, but this Canada could not grant us, because she has a protected system'and she was atraid of the competition of our better organized industries. Canada is at the parting of the
Of course, this has been referred to a great many times, and I am reading something which has been read before, but I purpose reading it even if it is disagreeable to my hon. friends on the other side of the House.
Ought we not, then, to arrange a commercial agreement with Canada if we can, by which we shall have direct access to her great supi>ly of natural products? They are coming. They are coming to the parting of the ways. Should we not now, therefore, before their policy has become too crystallized and fixed for change. . . greatly increase the natural resources available to our people?. . . by giving our people access to Canadian forests, we shall reduce the consumption of our own, which, in the hands of comparatively few owners, now have a value that requires the enlargement of our available timber resources.
He knew very well of our timber resources and that the time was not far distant when the United States would be compelled to pay practically whatever price we asked, and accept whatever terms we dictated for access to our natural resources. We are told by the Liberal party that the farmer will get more for his wheat under reciprocity, and that the lumberman will get fbore for his lumber. That may look very nice on the face of it. The lumberman will get more for his lumber this year- perhaps. I know some who have sold their year's cut, and they are going to divide $1.25 if this pact goes through. But in future years will it be our lumbermen on this side who will get the beneiit? Will it be the consumer who will get the benefit? No, it will be the great lumber interests that absolutely control the market in the United States, for, when they have control, they will pay us what they please.
I have wandered from the question of annexation, but here is something of President Taft's that brings me back to it:
The reduction in the . duties imposed by Canada will give us even a larger share of her market than we now enjoy, great as that is.
ways.
He still kept telling them that Canada was at the parting of the ways.
If we now neglect this opportunity to bring about closer business and trade relations, and insist upon the continuance of an artificial wall between the two countries, which differ no more in conditions of labour and production than do Kentucky and Tennessee or Georgia and Alabama, we shall throw away an opportunity for mutual benefit not likely to recur.
Finally, President Taft at New York at the end of April urged the editors, of the United States to support the agreement and used these words as the crowning reason why they should do it.
He went on the principle to strike while the iron was hot. He had these gentlemen on the run, and wanted to keep them on the run, and here is another thing he said:
X have said that this was a critical time in
the solution of the question of reciprocity. It is critical because, unless it is now decided, favourably to reciprocity, it is exceedingly probable that no such opportunity will ever again come to the United States. The forces which are at work in England and in Canada to separate her by a Chinese wall from the United States, and to make her part ot an imperial commercial band reaching from England around the world to England again, by a system of preferential tariffs, will derive an impetus from the rejection of this treaty, and if we would have reciprocity, with all the advantages that I have described and that 1 earnestly and sincerely believe will follow its adoption, we must take it now or give it up for ever.
He seems to think he can do more with the gentlemen in Canada who have charge of this pact than with his own people. But he is going to miss his mark if we are able to hold out, and I think we can. We are not going to let it pass, without an awful struggle; make no mistake about that. And when the hon, gentleman who leads the House (Mr. Fielding) makes us sit up to all hours of the night, makes us weary

of ourselves and of them, we will stay at it. And I hope that the people of Canada will give us credit for being earnest in our endeavours to keep from them this iniquitous pact that the government is trying to foist upon us. We have a right, and I do not suppose the hon. gentleman would deny it, to express our opinions upon the subject.
Another peculiar thing ia seen in this situation. I have had some parliamentary experience, but never, in any House that I have sat in, has a great measure been discussed without those who were responsible for it being in their places' all the time. It is all very well for hon. gentlemen opposite to make relays of their numbers to come and go. But they must not forget that they are responsible for the issue, and responsible for the waste of time since last November, and especially since last January, all because of the determination of two gentlemen who occupy the same position, plus the salary, that other members of the House do. It is all very well for them to tell us that they will freeze us out-or smoke us out, I do not know which-because they have their monthly allowance whereas we poor fellows will be at the end of onr tether soon. But we replenished our girmals before we left our homes. We have plenty to eat and drink, our families are not suffering because of the fact that we are here battling in the interests of the people of Canada. Now it is getting late, and I know that the hon. gentleman who leads the" House is weary, and I would ask him to consent to an adjournment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.

Motion agreed to.
On motion of Mr. Fielding, House adjourned at 11.31 p.m.
Monday, July 24, 1911.
